cards.idea: Real estate is land, what's permanently attached to it, and the rights of ownership. The business is every service built around it. Florida licenses activities, not job titles: what you do, and for whom, decides the license.
cards.scene: One house at 412 Cocoplum Way. A sales associate lists it, an appraiser values it, a loan originator arranges the mortgage, a title agent searches the record. All are in real estate. Only some need a real estate license.
cards.trap: The exam assumes everyone paid from the deal holds a real estate license. They don't. Appraisers, loan originators and title agents are regulated, but not by the real estate license and not by FREC.
cards.remember: Florida licenses what you do, not your job title.

question.q: In the sale of a house on Cocoplum Way, which person needs a Florida real estate license?
options: The appraiser valuing it for the lender
The loan originator arranging the mortgage
The sales associate who listed it
The title agent searching the record
question.why: Listing property for another is brokerage, which the real estate license covers. The others are regulated, but not by the real estate license or FREC.

cards.idea: Brokerage is bringing parties together to complete a deal, for pay. A sales associate works under a broker, in the broker's name, and is paid through that broker. Florida's license is the same for every specialization.
cards.scene: A Florida sales associate lists a house on Buttonwood Street on Monday and a strip center on Tuesday. Both are legal on one license. Her broker's supervision, not a second license, keeps her out of work she isn't ready for.
cards.trap: The exam offers "needs a commercial license to sell commercial property." Florida has none; one license covers both. It also offers "can open her own office once experienced." Opening a brokerage takes a broker's license.
cards.remember: One license covers homes and commercial. Running a brokerage needs a broker's license.

question.q: A sales associate who sells homes on Buttonwood Street is asked to list a strip center. What does Florida require?
options: A separate commercial real estate license
Nothing more; her license already covers it
A broker's license, since commercial is broker-only
Her own brokerage office for commercial work
question.why: Florida has no separate commercial license, so the same sales associate license covers both. Competence and her broker's supervision are what limit her.

cards.idea: Appraisal is an unbiased, standards-based estimate of value as of a specific date. Florida licenses appraisers separately, under Chapter 475, Part II, with their own board, not FREC. The appraiser's independence is the product.
cards.scene: The sales associate listing 1820 Marlberry Lane builds a thorough comparative market analysis from recent nearby sales, current listings and expired listings. She may do that, even be paid for it. Then she labels it "Appraisal." The label is the problem.
cards.trap: Two wrong answers. "A thorough CMA may be called an appraisal": no. "A licensee may never give an opinion of value": also no. Licensees give opinions of value every day. They just can't call them appraisals.
cards.remember: A CMA is fine, even paid. Never call it an appraisal.

question.q: The listing agent on Marlberry Lane prepares a CMA for the seller. Which is true under Florida law?
options: She may prepare it and be paid, but not call it an appraisal
She may not give any opinion of value
She may call it an appraisal if it is thorough enough
She needs the Appraisal Board's approval first
question.why: Florida lets a licensee prepare a CMA and even be paid for it, as long as it is never called an appraisal. Appraisers are licensed separately, under their own board.

cards.idea: A property manager runs property for an owner: tenants, rent, repairs, books, reports, under a written management agreement. In Florida, renting or leasing for another for pay is brokerage, so it generally needs a real estate license.
cards.scene: A duplex owner on Buttonwood Street pays a friend a percentage of the first month's rent to find tenants. The friend isn't "just helping." Finding tenants for another for compensation is brokerage, and doing it unlicensed is illegal.
cards.trap: The exam frames paid tenant-finding as a favor. Default answer: a license is required. Exemptions exist, such as certain salaried owner employees; check Chapter 2. Community association managers hold a different license entirely.
cards.remember: Leasing for another, for pay, is brokerage.

question.q: A duplex owner on Buttonwood Street pays a friend a share of the first month's rent for finding tenants. What is the friend doing?
options: Helping informally, so no license is needed
Acting as a community association manager
Nothing regulated, because no sale occurred
Brokerage activity that requires a license
question.why: Under Florida law, renting or leasing for another for compensation is brokerage. Without a license, the friend is acting illegally.

cards.idea: Financing covers who originates, funds, buys and services mortgage loans. Florida regulates mortgage brokering and loan origination under Chapter 494, through the Office of Financial Regulation, not DBPR and not FREC.
cards.scene: A sales associate selling a condo on Cocoplum Way tells the buyer, "I can arrange your mortgage too, for an extra fee." Her real estate license doesn't cover that. She may refer the buyer to lenders instead.
cards.trap: The exam suggests a real estate license covers arranging a loan for a fee. It doesn't; that's separately licensed. It also tempts you to name FREC or DBPR as the loan regulator. It's the Office of Financial Regulation.
cards.remember: Referring to lenders is fine. Arranging the loan for a fee is another license.

question.q: Which body regulates loan originators in Florida?
options: The Florida Real Estate Commission
The Office of Financial Regulation
The Division of Real Estate within DBPR
The Florida Real Estate Appraisal Board
question.why: Mortgage brokering and loan origination fall under Chapter 494 of the Florida Statutes, regulated by the Office of Financial Regulation. FREC and DBPR do not license them.

cards.idea: Development turns raw land into usable property: land acquisition, subdivision, construction, marketing. A subdivider divides land; a developer improves it. Florida licenses contractors separately, and local zoning controls what gets built.
cards.scene: A company buys 80 acres west of Marlberry Lane, records a plat dividing it into lots, and sells the empty lots to builders. It's a subdivider. It becomes a developer only if it adds roads, utilities or houses.
cards.trap: The exam treats subdivider and developer as the same. Dividing land with a recorded plat is subdividing; developing means improvements. Also: a custom builder builds to an owner's plans, a speculative builder builds first and sells later.
cards.remember: Subdivider divides. Developer improves.

question.q: A company records a plat dividing a tract west of Marlberry Lane into lots and sells them empty to builders. What is it?
options: A developer
A speculative builder
A subdivider
A custom builder
question.why: Dividing land into lots with a recorded plat is subdividing. It would be a developer only if it added improvements like roads, utilities or houses.

cards.idea: Counseling is expert real estate advice for a fee, paid whether or not a sale happens. That's what separates it from brokerage. Education, home inspection and title work are other fields, each under its own Florida rules.
cards.scene: An owner hires a real estate counselor to advise whether to sell, hold, lease, redevelop or exchange a property. The counselor is paid for the advice itself. If the owner decides to hold, the fee is still earned.
cards.trap: The exam says a counselor is paid only if the property sells. No. The fee is for the advice. A fee that depends on a sale is a brokerage fee, and collecting it requires a brokerage license.
cards.remember: Counselors are paid for advice. Sale-dependent fees are brokerage.

question.q: An owner hires a real estate counselor to advise whether to hold or sell. When is the counselor's fee earned?
options: Only if the owner decides to sell
Only once a buyer is under contract
Only if the advice raises the property's value
For the advice, whether or not a sale happens
question.why: A counselor is paid for the advice itself. A fee that depends on a sale is a brokerage fee and requires a brokerage license.

cards.idea: The textbook sorts real property into five categories by use: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural and special-purpose. Florida cares because later rules, like Chapter 4's residential-sales disclosures, depend on property type.
cards.scene: A duplex on Buttonwood Street is residential. A distribution warehouse at the edge of town is industrial. A retail store selling to the public is commercial. A church on Cocoplum Way, parking lot and office included, is special-purpose.
cards.trap: The exam dangles "commercial" for a warehouse because a business uses it. Storage and distribution make it industrial. It also calls a church commercial for its parking lot and office. It's special-purpose.
cards.remember: Warehouse is industrial. Church is special-purpose. Selling to the public is commercial.

question.q: A distribution warehouse used for storage sits at the edge of town. Which category is it?
options: Industrial
Commercial
Special-purpose
Agricultural
question.why: Warehousing and distribution are industrial uses. A business using the building doesn't make it commercial; selling to the public would.

items.title: The Florida regulators, at a first look

cards.idea: Chapter 475 and FREC's rules in Chapter 61J2 govern licensing. DBPR's Division of Real Estate is the machinery: applications, licenses, records, investigations. FREC, appointed by the Governor, makes rules, decides qualifications and imposes discipline.
cards.scene: A complaint about a sales associate reaches the state. A DBPR investigator looks into it. FREC decides the penalty. Had the complaint been about an appraiser or a loan originator, FREC wouldn't be involved at all.
cards.trap: Two swaps. "FREC regulates appraisers" or "FREC licenses mortgage brokers": neither. And department versus commission: investigating a complaint is DBPR's job. Deciding the penalty is FREC's.
cards.remember: DBPR investigates. FREC makes rules and decides penalties.

question.q: A buyer complains that a sales associate misled her. Who decides the penalty?
options: The Division of Real Estate's investigators
The Office of Financial Regulation
The Florida Real Estate Commission
The local REALTOR® association
question.why: Investigating a complaint is the department's job, but deciding the penalty is the commission's. FREC is the rule-making and judging body.

cards.idea: Trade associations are voluntary, and none is a government body. Only NAR members may use REALTOR®, a membership mark NAR owns; members follow its Code of Ethics. NAREB members use Realtist. Florida's state association is Florida Realtors.
cards.scene: A sales associate on Marlberry Lane advertises herself as a REALTOR® but never joined the association. Her license is real; the title isn't. She's misrepresenting herself, a separate problem under Florida law.
cards.trap: The exam says every Florida licensee is a REALTOR®. Only association members are. It also says FREC disciplines Code of Ethics violations. FREC enforces Florida law; the Code is a private standard.
cards.remember: REALTOR® means membership, not licensure. FREC doesn't enforce NAR's code.

question.q: A Florida licensee breaks the REALTOR® Code of Ethics but no Florida law or FREC rule. What can FREC do about the Code breach?
options: Suspend the license for the Code breach
Nothing; FREC enforces Florida law, not the Code
Order DBPR to revoke the license
Fine the licensee under its own rules
question.why: NAR's Code of Ethics is a private standard; breaking it can cost association membership. FREC enforces Chapter 475 and its own rules.

cards.idea: A designation is a credential an organization awards for completing its courses and experience requirements. It shows specialty training. It isn't a license and adds no legal authority. An MAI doesn't make someone a Florida-certified appraiser.
cards.scene: A property manager with the CPM designation, but no Florida real estate license, offers to lease units at a building on Buttonwood Street for a percentage of the rent. Impressive credential. Still not a license.
cards.trap: The exam offers the designation as enough to do licensed work. It never is. Leasing for others for pay still requires a Florida real estate license, unless a Florida exemption applies.
cards.remember: A designation is training, never a license.

question.q: A CPM holder with no Florida real estate license offers to lease units on Buttonwood Street for a percentage of the rent. Which is true?
options: The CPM lets her lease units for others
She may lease if she also holds the GRI
She may lease units but not collect rent
She needs a license unless an exemption applies
question.why: A designation adds no legal authority. Leasing for others for compensation still requires a Florida real estate license unless an exemption applies.

2.name: License Law and Qualifications for Licensure

cards.idea: A home sale is big money, done rarely, with unequal knowledge. So Florida licenses practitioners under Chapter 475, Part I, using its police power, to protect the public. A license is a privilege the state can take back.
cards.scene: A first-time buyer sits across from a seasoned licensee: the largest purchase of her life, made rarely, knowing far less than the professional. That gap is exactly why Florida licenses the professional.
cards.trap: The exam offers "maintain high commission rates," "limit competition" or "protect licensees from unqualified competitors." All plausible, all wrong. The purpose is protecting the public.
cards.remember: License law protects the public, under the state's police power.

question.q: What is the stated purpose of Florida's real estate license law?
options: To protect the public
To limit the number of agents
To protect licensees from unqualified competitors
To maintain high commission rates
question.why: Florida licenses practitioners to protect the public, under its police power. The other choices describe protecting the profession, which is not the purpose.

items.title: What counts as real estate services

cards.idea: Florida defines a broker by what they do: for another, for compensation, selling, buying, renting, leasing, exchanging, appraising, auctioning, advertising or procuring parties. Offering or attempting counts. It reaches business opportunities, not just land.
cards.scene: Someone shows a house on Pond Apple Road to three prospects for a promised fee. No offer comes. Someone else finds a buyer for a dry cleaner on Strangler Fig Avenue for a fee. Both performed real estate services.
cards.trap: The exam says "the deal never closed, so no license was needed." Wrong; offering and attempting count. It also implies selling a business isn't real estate. Business opportunities are covered even when no real property changes hands.
cards.remember: Attempting counts. Business opportunities count.

question.q: For a promised fee, an unlicensed person shows a house on Pond Apple Road to three prospects. No offer is made. Did he perform real estate services?
options: No, because no deal closed
No, because he was never actually paid
Yes, because attempting a sale for a fee counts
Only if the seller signed a listing agreement
question.why: Florida's definition covers offering and attempting, for compensation paid, promised or expected. A deal doesn't have to close.

cards.idea: The definition bites only for compensation, read broadly: anything of value, direct or indirect, before or after, even just expected. It must also be "for another," which is why owners are exempt. One transaction is enough.
cards.scene: A homeowner on Wax Myrtle Lane promises a neighbor his boat if the neighbor finds a buyer. The neighbor brings one, and the boat, a scenario value of $15,000, changes hands. That's unlicensed brokerage.
cards.trap: The exam tries "it was only one sale" and "I took a boat, not money." Both fail. The flip side is tested too: a friend who helps free, with nothing promised or expected, needs no license.
cards.remember: Anything of value counts, and one deal is enough.

question.q: A neighbor on Wax Myrtle Lane finds a buyer for a friend's house and receives the friend's boat. It is his only deal ever. Did he need a license?
options: No, because a boat isn't compensation
No, because it was a single transaction
Only if the boat's value passed a set amount
Yes, because a boat is valuable consideration
question.why: Valuable consideration includes anything of value, and Florida has no one-time exception. He acted for another and procured a buyer.

cards.idea: Some do brokerage-like acts unlicensed: owners with their own property, attorneys doing legal work, attorneys in fact signing documents, court-appointed fiduciaries, salaried on-site apartment leasing employees, cemetery lot sellers. Each exemption stops where its reason stops.
cards.scene: A son with power of attorney signs the listing and the deed for his mother's rental house on Beautyberry Court. Exempt. A neighbor then offers him a fee to find a buyer for her condo. That needs a license.
cards.trap: The exam stretches an exemption past its reason: the attorney taking a finder's fee with no legal work, the attorney in fact finding buyers, the apartment employee showing another owner's complex. Each needs a license.
cards.remember: An exemption covers only the activity that justifies it.

question.q: A son holds power of attorney for his mother's house on Beautyberry Court. Which act is exempt?
options: Signing the deed on his mother's behalf
Finding a buyer for a neighbor's condo for a fee
Taking a finder's fee for introducing a buyer
Marketing friends' homes for a share of the price
question.why: A power of attorney lets him sign contracts and conveyances for his mother. It doesn't let him find buyers for others for a fee.

cards.idea: Florida issues three individual licenses. A sales associate works only under an employing broker. A broker runs the brokerage, holds escrow and is paid by the public. A broker associate holds a broker's license but works under another broker.
cards.scene: A grateful seller offers a sales associate at a brokerage on Strangler Fig Avenue a direct bonus. She must decline it or have it paid through her broker. Only her employing broker may pay her for brokerage work.
cards.trap: The exam treats "broker associate" as a lower license, or a sales associate with a fancier title. It's a full broker's license held by someone who chooses to work under another broker.
cards.remember: Broker associate: a broker's license, working under another broker.

question.q: Which best describes a broker associate?
options: A sales associate with extra experience
A person with a broker's license working under another broker
A temporary license held before the broker exam
A broker who employs sales associates
question.why: A broker associate holds a full broker's license but chooses to work under another broker, the way a sales associate does.

items.title: Qualifying for a sales associate license

cards.idea: To qualify, you must be at least 18, hold a high school diploma or equivalent, pass the 63-hour pre-license course's end-of-course exam, be honest and of good character, and pass the state exam.
cards.scene: A recent graduate on Pond Apple Road finishes the 63-hour course a month after turning 18. She meets the age and education requirements. Her license now depends on the application, the background check and the state exam.
cards.trap: The exam blurs the course exam and the state exam. Passing the end-of-course exam makes you eligible. It doesn't license you. The state exam is a separate test given by the state's testing vendor.
cards.remember: Course exam makes you eligible. State exam gets the license.

question.q: A student on Pond Apple Road passes the end-of-course exam for the 63-hour course. What is her status?
options: Licensed, pending her broker's signature
Licensed as an inactive sales associate
Eligible to practice under a broker's supervision
Eligible for the state exam, not yet licensed
question.why: Passing the course exam makes her eligible but doesn't license her. The state exam is a separate test.

cards.idea: Applicants file with DBPR and submit electronic fingerprints for a state and federal background check. They must answer truthfully. A record doesn't automatically bar a license; FREC weighs it. Lying is what sinks applicants.
cards.scene: An applicant on Wax Myrtle Lane pled no contest to a misdemeanor eight years ago, and adjudication was withheld. He leaves the question blank: "I was never convicted." The background check finds it. The omission is the problem.
cards.trap: The exam says withheld adjudication means nothing to disclose. Wrong: guilty pleas, no contest pleas and withheld adjudication must be disclosed. It also says any record disqualifies. No; FREC weighs it.
cards.remember: Disclose everything. Concealment hurts more than the record.

question.q: An applicant pled no contest to a misdemeanor and adjudication was withheld. What must he do on the application?
options: Leave it off, since he wasn't convicted
Withdraw, since any record disqualifies him
Disclose it truthfully
Disclose it only if it was a felony
question.why: On the Florida application, no contest pleas and withheld adjudication must be disclosed. Concealment is itself evidence the applicant isn't honest and trustworthy.

cards.idea: Once the application is approved, the applicant takes the state exam: 100 questions, passing score 75. Passing issues the license, but a sales associate's license is active only when tied to an employing broker.
cards.scene: A new licensee passes on a Tuesday. On Wednesday she shows a friend's listing on Beautyberry Court before any broker has registered her. She holds a license, but she had no right to perform services that day.
cards.trap: The exam treats "passed the exam" as "may now practice." Practice requires an active license under an employing broker. Know the numbers cold: 100 questions, 75 to pass.
cards.remember: Passing licenses you. A broker makes it active.

question.q: A new licensee passed the state exam yesterday but has no employing broker. May she show a listing on Beautyberry Court today?
options: No, she needs an active license under an employing broker
Yes, the license is active once issued
Yes, if the seller agrees in writing
No, she must first finish post-licensing education
question.why: A sales associate's license is active only when tied to an employing broker. Without one, she holds a license but cannot practice.

cards.idea: Before the first renewal, a sales associate must complete 45 hours of post-licensing education and pass its exam; a broker, 60. Miss it and the license is null and void. It replaces regular CE that first cycle.
cards.scene: A sales associate on Pond Apple Road has a strong first year and keeps putting off the post-licensing course. The first renewal deadline passes. Her closings next week now involve a person who holds no license.
cards.trap: The exam swaps "void" for "inactive." An inactive license can be reactivated. A void license is gone. It also swaps the hours: 45 for a sales associate, 60 for a broker.
cards.remember: Miss post-licensing by first renewal: license void. 45 sales, 60 broker.

question.q: A sales associate misses the post-licensing course before her first renewal. What happens to her license?
options: It becomes involuntarily inactive
It is suspended until she finishes
It becomes null and void
It renews if she pays a late fee
question.why: Missing post-licensing before the first renewal makes the license null and void. It ceases to exist rather than going inactive.

cards.idea: After the first renewal, each two-year cycle requires 14 hours of continuing education, including Core Law. Chapter 475 and FREC's rules change, and Core Law makes every licensee hear what changed, every cycle.
cards.scene: A broker associate on Strangler Fig Avenue finished post-licensing two years ago. For this renewal she needs the 14 hours, Core Law included. Last cycle's post-licensing course doesn't count toward this one.
cards.trap: The sequence. First renewal: post-licensing, no regular CE. Every renewal after: 14 hours of CE. The exam offers "14 hours plus post-licensing at first renewal" and "14 hours starting with first renewal." Both wrong.
cards.remember: Post-licensing first. Then 14 hours, with Core Law, every cycle.

question.q: What does a sales associate owe at her first renewal?
options: 14 hours of CE plus post-licensing
14 hours of CE only
Core Law only
Post-licensing only, no regular CE
question.why: Post-licensing replaces continuing education at the first renewal. The 14 hours of CE start with the renewal after that.

cards.idea: You needn't live in Florida to hold a Florida license. Nonresidents from states with mutual recognition agreements skip the pre-license course and full exam, but still pass a shorter Florida law exam and the background check.
cards.scene: A broker licensed and living in another state wants to list a client's vacation condo on Beautyberry Court. If her state has a mutual recognition agreement, she takes the Florida law exam. Either way, she needs a Florida license.
cards.trap: The exam says "mutual recognition means no exam." There's still an exam, on Florida law. And mutual recognition is for nonresidents. It isn't a back door for someone already living in Florida.
cards.remember: Mutual recognition: nonresidents only, and still a Florida law exam.

question.q: A broker licensed in a mutual recognition state, and living there, wants a Florida license. What must she do?
options: Nothing; her license is valid in Florida
Pass an exam on Florida real estate law
Take the pre-license course and full exam
Move to Florida first
question.why: Mutual recognition lets her skip the pre-license course and full state exam, but she still passes an exam on Florida law and meets the other requirements.

cards.idea: Performing real estate services for pay without a valid, active license is a third-degree felony in Florida. An unlicensed person can't sue to collect a commission, and a licensee who pays one commits a violation too.
cards.scene: A sales associate on Wax Myrtle Lane lets her unlicensed brother-in-law show listings on weekends and splits commissions with him. He commits a felony. She violates the license law by paying him. If she stops paying, he can't sue.
cards.trap: The exam offers "second-degree misdemeanor," since most license-law violations are misdemeanors. Unlicensed practice is the exception: a third-degree felony. Working on a void or inactive license counts as unlicensed too.
cards.remember: Unlicensed practice is a third-degree felony.

question.q: An unlicensed person shows homes on weekends for a share of a licensee's commissions. What offense is he committing?
options: A second-degree misdemeanor
A first-degree misdemeanor
A third-degree felony
No offense, since the licensee pays him
question.why: Performing real estate services for compensation without a license is a third-degree felony in Florida. Most license-law violations are misdemeanors; this one is the exception.

items.title: Two bodies, one job: DBPR and FREC

cards.idea: DBPR is the state agency; its Division of Real Estate processes applications, issues licenses, keeps records and investigates. FREC sets policy and decides: seven members, appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the Senate.
cards.scene: A buyer on Paurotis Drive thinks a listing agent pocketed part of her deposit. She files with DBPR, whose investigator gathers documents and interviews. Whether the agent is disciplined, and how severely, is FREC's decision.
cards.trap: The exam reverses roles: "FREC investigates" or "DBPR revokes licenses." Both wrong. It also offers "five brokers and two consumers." FREC is four brokers, one broker or sales associate, two consumer members.
cards.remember: DBPR investigates. FREC makes rules and disciplines.

question.q: Which describes FREC's seven members?
options: Five brokers and two consumer members
Four brokers, one broker or sales associate, two consumer members
Seven licensed brokers
Four brokers and three consumer members
question.why: FREC has four brokers, one broker or sales associate, and two consumer members who have never been brokers or sales associates.

items.title: Where the rules live: Chapter 475 and Rule 61J2

cards.idea: Three layers. Chapter 475 is the license law. Chapter 455 governs every DBPR profession. Rule 61J2 is FREC's rule book, adopted under Chapter 120 with public notice and comment. Breaking a rule violates the license law.
cards.scene: A sales associate on Pigeon Plum Street reads Chapter 475 front to back, finds nothing on how a trade name must appear on a sign, and decides there's no requirement. There is. It's in the rules, not the statute.
cards.trap: The exam treats rules as weaker than the statute. A rule can't override a statute, but within its scope it binds licensees exactly as the statute does. And who adopts the rules? FREC.
cards.remember: FREC's rules bind licensees like the statute itself.

question.q: A licensee breaks a FREC rule in Chapter 61J2 on conduct the statute never mentions. What is the result?
options: No violation, since only statutes bind
A violation only if the Legislature approves the rule
A violation of the license law
A warning, since rules are advisory
question.why: Breaking a Commission rule is itself a violation of the license law. Within its scope, a FREC rule binds exactly as the statute does.

items.title: What a license can be: active, inactive, null and void

cards.idea: Active means you may practice; associates need an employing broker. Voluntary inactive is chosen and kept renewed. Involuntary inactive follows a missed renewal and can be revived within 2 years. Null and void means gone.
cards.scene: A sales associate on Simpson Stopper Way takes a year off, requests inactive status and keeps renewing: voluntary inactive. Her colleague forgets to renew: involuntarily inactive the next day, null and void if two years pass unreactivated.
cards.trap: The exam blurs "inactive." Cause decides it: choice is voluntary, missed renewal is involuntary, even if he meant to quit. And an involuntarily inactive licensee who keeps showing houses is practicing without an active license.
cards.remember: Missed renewal: involuntary inactive. Two years unrevived: null and void.

question.q: A licensee on Simpson Stopper Way forgets to renew and does nothing to reactivate for more than 2 years. What is his license's status?
options: Null and void
Involuntarily inactive
Voluntarily inactive
Active but delinquent
question.why: A missed renewal makes the license involuntarily inactive. Left unreactivated past 2 years, it becomes null and void.

items.title: Renewal and education across the license cycle

cards.idea: Licenses run on a two-year cycle, expiring March 31 or September 30. First renewal requires post-licensing; missing it voids the license. Later renewals need 14 hours of CE; missing them makes the license involuntarily inactive.
cards.scene: At the Paurotis Drive office, a broker associate has 11 of 14 hours done before a September 30 expiration. Miss it, and on October 1 she's involuntarily inactive. A sales associate who never started post-licensing is null and void.
cards.trap: The exam mixes up three courses. Pre-licensing, 63 hours, gets you to the exam. Post-licensing, 45 hours, missed voids the license. CE, 14 hours, missed means involuntary inactive. Renewal is due by expiration, not after.
cards.remember: Miss post-licensing: void. Miss CE: involuntarily inactive.

question.q: A broker associate past her first renewal hasn't finished her 14 CE hours by her September 30 expiration. What is her status on October 1?
options: Null and void
Suspended pending a hearing
Voluntarily inactive
Involuntarily inactive
question.why: Missing CE at a later renewal makes the license involuntarily inactive, which can be reactivated. Only missing post-licensing at the first renewal voids it.

cards.idea: Licensees must notify the Commission within 10 days of changing their mailing address, and associates within 10 days of changing employers. DBPR notices sent to the last address on file count as properly served.
cards.scene: A sales associate leaves the Pigeon Plum Street brokerage Friday, starts at a Simpson Stopper Way firm Monday, and plans to "get to the paperwork." Wednesday he writes an offer. Unrecorded, he isn't registered with that broker.
cards.trap: The exam treats an address change as just mail. It governs service of legal notices; a complaint sent to your old address still binds you. Also, a departing associate can't keep working the old broker's clients.
cards.remember: Ten days to report a new address or a new employer.

question.q: A licensee moves and doesn't update her address. A complaint is sent to the old address. Which is true?
options: The notice is invalid until she receives it
She is bound, because notice to the address on file counts
DBPR must re-serve her at her new address
She has 10 days after learning of it to object
question.why: Florida law treats DBPR notices sent to the last address on file as properly served. Not receiving it because it went to an old address is no defense.

items.title: Registering a brokerage that is a company

cards.idea: People are licensed; brokerage companies are registered. Every registered entity needs an active broker at the top, and anyone in it performing real estate services must be licensed. Owning shares requires no license.
cards.scene: Three friends form an LLC to open a brokerage on Necklace Pod Lane: a broker, a sales associate and an unlicensed investor. The broker is the required member or manager. The investor may own a share. The sales associate can't run it.
cards.trap: The exam says "the company is licensed." Companies are registered; people are licensed. It also dangles the investor-owner who starts negotiating a deal for a commission. Ownership needed no license. That activity does.
cards.remember: Companies register. People are licensed. An active broker sits at the top.

question.q: In a brokerage organized as a limited partnership, who must be an active broker?
options: Every limited partner
Only the largest investor
At least one general partner
Every partner, general or limited
question.why: A limited partnership needs at least one general partner who is an active broker. Limited partners, who invest but don't manage, need no license.

cards.idea: A broker may operate under a trade name registered with the Commission, shown on the license and used consistently. The name links the public to the accountable broker. A sales associate can't have a trade name.
cards.scene: A broker on Paurotis Drive registers "Paurotis Coastal Realty." Two years later she advertises as "Paurotis Luxury Homes" without registering it. Maybe a better brand. Until it's registered, using it is the violation.
cards.trap: The exam says a sales associate may register a trade name with the broker's approval. No; the business belongs to the broker. Also, fictitious-name registration with the Department of State doesn't replace Commission registration.
cards.remember: Register the name with the Commission before using it. Brokers only.

question.q: A sales associate wants her own trade name, and her broker approves. May she register one?
options: Yes, with written broker approval
Yes, if it is filed with the Department of State
Yes, if it includes the broker's name
No, a sales associate cannot have a trade name
question.why: A sales associate cannot operate a brokerage, so she cannot have a trade name for one. The license and the business belong to the broker.

cards.idea: Associates work for one employer at a time. A broker may hold multiple licenses, one for each brokerage entity they serve as the required broker. An associate's only exception is a group license, for related owner-developer entities.
cards.scene: A developer's three related companies build subdivisions off Simpson Stopper Way, Necklace Pod Lane and Pigeon Plum Street. One sales associate sells in all three under a group license. An unrelated homeowner's resale down the road isn't covered.
cards.trap: The exam offers "a sales associate may work for two brokers if both consent." Consent doesn't create a second employer. It also swaps multiple licenses, a broker's, with a group license, an associate's.
cards.remember: Group license: one associate, related owner-developers, their own properties only.

question.q: A sales associate's two unrelated brokers both consent to her working for each of them. Which is true?
options: She may, since both brokers consented
She may, if she obtains a group license
She may not; consent doesn't create a second employer
She may, if she holds multiple licenses
question.why: An associate works for one employer at a time. The only exception, a group license, covers related owner-developer entities, not unrelated brokers.

items.title: Agency basics: principal, customer and fiduciary

cards.idea: An agent works for a principal as a fiduciary, putting that principal first. Everyone else in the deal is a customer: dealt with honestly, not represented. Florida adds a twist: single agency exists only in writing.
cards.scene: A buyer talks to a licensee for weeks and starts calling her his agent. Nothing is signed. He doesn't have a single agent. He is far more likely dealing with a transaction broker.
cards.trap: The casual word "agent." Under Chapter 475 what counts is which authorized relationship the licensee is in. Fiduciary duties come only from single agency, never from the buyer feeling represented.
cards.remember: No writing, no single agency. Fiduciary duties come only from single agency.

question.q: For weeks a buyer discusses homes on Firewheel Road with a licensee and calls her "my agent." Nothing was ever signed. What relationship most likely exists?
options: Single agency, implied from their conduct
Transaction broker
No relationship, so she owes him nothing
Dual agency, since she also talks to sellers
question.why: Florida requires single agency to be established in writing, so conduct alone doesn't create it and the licensee is presumed a transaction broker. Implied agency is the generic-textbook answer that Florida narrows.

cards.idea: These labels measure scope of authority. Universal: almost anything the principal could do, like a broad durable power of attorney. General: ongoing authority across a continuing course of business. Special: one task, ending when it's done.
cards.scene: A sales associate takes the listing on 2210 Fiddlewood Avenue. Her broker is a special agent of that seller, for that one listing. She is a general agent of the broker, so the broker answers for her conduct.
cards.trap: Both labels apply at once, in the same deal. Asked what kind of agent the associate who took the listing is, the exam hopes you say special agent. The answer is general agent of the broker.
cards.remember: Broker: special agent of the seller. Associate: general agent of the broker.

question.q: A sales associate takes the listing on 2210 Fiddlewood Avenue for her employing broker. What kind of agent is the sales associate?
options: Special agent of the seller
Universal agent of the seller
Special agent of the broker
General agent of the broker
question.why: A sales associate is a general agent of the employing broker, with ongoing authority in the broker's business. The listing broker is the seller's special agent, which is why "special agent of the seller" tempts.

items.title: The three authorized relationships, and whose relationship it is

cards.idea: Florida allows exactly three relationships with a buyer or seller: transaction broker, single agent, or no brokerage relationship. Each one belongs to the brokerage, not to the sales associate, who acts in the broker's name.
cards.scene: One associate at a firm is single agent for a seller. A colleague in the same office wants to be single agent for the buyer of that same property. She can't. The whole firm is already the seller's single agent.
cards.trap: Treating the associate as the party to the relationship. "She decided to become the buyer's single agent while her colleague kept the listing" describes something the firm cannot do in a residential sale.
cards.remember: Three relationships only, and the firm holds them, not the person.

question.q: One associate holds a single-agent listing on a house at 905 Firewheel Road. A colleague in the same office wants to be the buyer's single agent for that house. May she?
options: No, the firm already holds the seller's single agency
Yes, if both associates disclose it in writing
Yes, each associate holds their own relationship
Yes, if the broker approves it verbally
question.why: The relationship is between the brokerage and the customer, so the whole firm is the seller's single agent. Treating each associate as a separate party to the relationship is the trap.

cards.idea: A transaction broker gives limited representation to the buyer, the seller, or both, and advocates for neither. Florida presumes every licensee is one unless single agency or no brokerage relationship is set up in writing.
cards.scene: 418 Saw Palmetto Trail is listed at $465,000. The seller privately says $440,000 is fine; the buyer privately could stretch to $455,000. The transaction broker presents his $435,000 offer promptly. Neither private number crosses the table.
cards.trap: Limited confidentiality is not limited honesty. Price, terms and motive stay back; a known material defect never does. And a question with no written disclosure at all wants "transaction broker," because of the presumption.
cards.remember: Put nothing in writing and you're a transaction broker.

question.q: A licensee helps a buyer find and buy a home on Saw Palmetto Trail. No disclosure of any kind was ever signed. What relationship existed?
options: Transaction broker, by presumption
Single agent, implied from the work she did
No brokerage relationship, since nothing was signed
None, so the licensee acted unlawfully
question.why: All licensees are presumed to be transaction brokers unless single agency or no brokerage relationship is established in writing. "Nothing signed" points to the default, not to no brokerage relationship, which itself needs a written notice.

items.title: Single agent and its nine duties

cards.idea: A single agent represents the buyer or the seller, never both, as a full fiduciary. Nine duties, including loyalty, confidentiality, obedience and full disclosure. It must be established in writing through the single agent notice.
cards.scene: A buyer touring 1307 Spanish Stopper Drive says he's already sold his house and must close fast. He's a customer, so the listing associate tells the seller. She still can't tell him the house never flooded if she knows it did.
cards.trap: The exam pits duties against each other. Obedience never excuses dishonesty, and confidentiality never covers a known material defect. A seller's "don't mention the cracked slab" is an instruction the single agent can't follow.
cards.remember: Obedience and confidentiality stop where a known material defect begins.

question.q: A licensee is single agent for the seller of 1307 Spanish Stopper Drive. A touring buyer volunteers that he has sold his house and must close fast. What should she do with that fact?
options: Tell the seller, under full disclosure
Keep it private, since the buyer told her directly
Ignore it, since customers' statements don't matter
Share it only with the buyer's written permission
question.why: The buyer is a customer, and the single agent owes her principal full disclosure, including what a customer lets slip. Confidentiality runs to the principal, not to the customer.

items.title: Consent to transition to transaction broker

cards.idea: A single agent may step down to transaction broker, but only with the principal's written consent before the change. Florida built this for in-house sales, so a firm with both sides never becomes a dual agent.
cards.scene: A firm is single agent for the seller of 905 Firewheel Road. A buyer working with another associate in the same office wants to offer. If the seller signed the consent, the firm becomes transaction broker for both.
cards.trap: The word "before." Consent signed after the firm has already acted as transaction broker for both sides doesn't cure that earlier period. And the transition never creates dual agency; it exists to prevent it.
cards.remember: Written consent first, then the switch. Never the other way round.

question.q: A firm with a single-agent listing on 905 Firewheel Road acted as transaction broker for both sides for two weeks, then got the seller's written consent to transition. Does that cure the two weeks?
options: Yes, written consent applies back to the start
No, consent must be signed before the change
Yes, if the buyer signs it too
Yes, as long as the sale hasn't closed
question.why: The principal's written consent must come before the change. Consent after the firm was already acting as transaction broker doesn't cure the period without it.

cards.idea: A licensee can deal with a buyer or seller while representing no one. It must be set up in writing with the no brokerage relationship notice. No loyalty, obedience or confidentiality of any kind.
cards.scene: A licensee brings a buyer to a for-sale-by-owner house. She has no agreement with the owner, and the buyer doesn't want representation. She still deals honestly, accounts for funds and discloses known material defects.
cards.trap: Reading "no brokerage relationship" as "no duties." Honesty, accounting for funds and disclosure of known material defects in residential property remain. Those three appear in all three relationship lists.
cards.remember: No relationship still means honesty, accounting and defect disclosure.

question.q: With a written no brokerage relationship notice, a licensee brings a buyer to a for-sale-by-owner home on Spanish Stopper Drive. She knows it floods, which isn't visible. What does she owe the buyer?
options: Nothing, because she represents no one
Silence unless the owner agrees to disclose
Disclosure only if she has an agreement with the owner
Disclosure of the flooding
question.why: Even with no brokerage relationship, the licensee must disclose known facts that materially affect value and aren't readily observable. Reading "no brokerage relationship" as "no duties" is the trap.

cards.idea: In a nonresidential deal, a broker can designate one associate as single agent for the buyer and another for the seller, inside the same firm. Both parties must request it in writing and meet a statutory asset threshold.
cards.scene: A large firm has both sides of a nonresidential sale. Each sophisticated party wants its own advocate. With written requests and the asset threshold met, one associate represents the buyer, another the seller.
cards.trap: Carrying it into a residential sale. A question set at a three-bedroom house on Fiddlewood Avenue that offers "designated sales associates" is offering a wrong answer. Residential sales never qualify.
cards.remember: Designated sales associates: nonresidential only, requested in writing.

question.q: The buyer and seller of a three-bedroom house on Fiddlewood Avenue both work with one firm. No single agency exists yet. Each wants an advocate. What can the firm lawfully offer both?
options: Transaction broker representation for both
Designated sales associates for each party
Disclosed dual agency with written consent
Separate single agents from the same office
question.why: Designated sales associates are never available in a residential sale, so a firm working both sides can only be a transaction broker. Offering "designated sales associates" for a house is the trap answer.

items.title: Dual agency: not an authorized relationship

cards.idea: A dual agent represents both buyer and seller as a fiduciary in the same deal. Florida bans it, disclosed or not. One fiduciary can't chase the highest price and the lowest price at once.
cards.scene: A licensee is already single agent for a seller, and a buyer wants her as his full agent too. Florida's answer: she becomes transaction broker for both, through the seller's written consent to transition.
cards.trap: Both parties "agreed in writing" to let one licensee be full agent for both. Many other states allow that, which is why it tempts. Consent doesn't make dual agency lawful in Florida.
cards.remember: Dual agency is illegal in Florida, even with everyone's written consent.

question.q: The buyer and seller of a home on Saw Palmetto Trail both agree in writing to let one licensee be a full fiduciary for both. Under Florida law, what is true?
options: It's not permitted; the licensee should be a transaction broker
It's lawful only in a nonresidential sale
It's lawful because both consented in writing
It's lawful if the broker approves it
question.why: Florida forbids dual agency whether disclosed or not, and consent doesn't fix it. Many other states allow disclosed dual agency, which makes the "both consented" answer feel right.

cards.idea: The Act's disclosures apply to residential sales: improved property of four or fewer units, unimproved land intended for four or fewer, or agricultural property of 10 or fewer acres. Nonresidential deals, auctions and appraisals are exempt.
cards.scene: A licensee hosts an open house on Saw Palmetto Trail, greeting visitors and handing out the property sheet. No notice needed. Then she asks a visitor what he could really afford. Now the exemption is gone.
cards.trap: Treating every open house as exempt. The exemption holds only while the licensee isn't eliciting confidential information, signing agreements or negotiating. Exemptions are defined by what the licensee doesn't do.
cards.remember: Residential sale: four or fewer units, or 10 or fewer agricultural acres.

question.q: At an open house on Saw Palmetto Trail, a licensee hands out property sheets, then asks a visitor what he could really afford. What is the effect?
options: None; open houses are always exempt
The exemption is lost once she elicits confidential information
The exemption is lost only if a contract is signed
She automatically becomes the visitor's single agent
question.why: The open house exemption covers only showings that don't involve eliciting confidential information, signing agreements or negotiating. Asking what he can really afford is eliciting confidential information, so the exemption is gone.

items.title: When the notice is given, and how long it is kept

cards.idea: The single agent notice comes before or at the listing or representation agreement, or before showing property, whichever occurs first. Transaction broker needs no notice. Brokers keep disclosure documents 5 years for residential deals with a written contract.
cards.scene: A buyer's licensee shows a house on Spanish Stopper Drive on Saturday and plans to sign the representation agreement Monday. The showing comes first, so the single agent notice was due before Saturday's showing.
cards.trap: "A transaction broker must disclose in writing before showing property." Older forms had a transaction broker notice, so it looks familiar. Under current Florida law it's the presumed relationship and needs none.
cards.remember: Single agent notice: before the agreement or the showing, whichever comes first.

question.q: A buyer's licensee shows a buyer the house on Spanish Stopper Drive on Saturday and plans to sign the representation agreement Monday. When was the single agent notice due?
options: At Monday's signing
Before any offer is written
At closing
Before Saturday's showing
question.why: The notice is due before or at the representation agreement, or before showing property, whichever occurs first. The showing came first, so Monday was too late.

items.title: Material defects: what every licensee owes the buyer

cards.idea: Every licensee must disclose known facts that materially affect residential value and aren't readily observable. Johnson v. Davis puts the same duty on sellers, and an "as is" clause doesn't excuse it.
cards.scene: The seller of 2416 Fiddlewood Avenue says the back bedroom flooded in the last two big storms, now hidden under new flooring. Listed "as is" at $389,000. The buyer asks nothing about water. The licensee must disclose it.
cards.trap: "The buyer had an inspection, so the licensee was off the hook." No: an inspection that missed it doesn't cancel what the licensee knew. Also wrong: transaction brokers or no-relationship licensees don't owe this duty.
cards.remember: Known, material, hidden: disclose it, whatever the relationship or the contract.

question.q: A licensee knows a ceiling leak was painted over before listing. The buyer's inspection misses it. Must the licensee still disclose the leak?
options: Yes, the inspection doesn't cancel her duty
No, the inspection shifted the burden to the buyer
No, a painted-over leak is readily observable
Only if she is the buyer's single agent
question.why: An inspection that missed a hidden defect doesn't cancel the licensee's duty to disclose what she knows. All three relationships owe this duty, so it doesn't depend on being a single agent.

cards.idea: Every active broker must keep a registered office, with an entrance sign readable from outside naming the broker, any trade name, and that it's a real estate business. The public must be able to find whoever is accountable.
cards.scene: A broker runs the business from a spare bedroom on Sawgrass Court and meets clients at coffee shops. Working from home is fine if zoning allows. No registered office and no sign is the violation.
cards.trap: The associate who rents a storefront, calls it a "desk" and puts their own name over the door. A sales associate may not maintain an office. Their name can go on the sign only underneath the broker's.
cards.remember: Brokers keep a registered office with a sign. Associates never keep their own.

question.q: A broker runs the business from a spare bedroom on Sawgrass Court, meets clients at coffee shops, and has no registered office and no sign. What is the violation?
options: Running a brokerage out of a residence
Meeting clients away from the office
Having no registered office with a sign at the entrance
None, because a sign is required only for storefront offices
question.why: A broker's office can be in a residence if local zoning allows it, but it must exist, be registered, and carry a sign readable from outside. The tempting answer blames working from home, which is allowed.

cards.idea: Any additional location where the brokerage does business is a branch office, registered separately with its own fee and its own sign. A subdivision sales shelter used only for that subdivision isn't one.
cards.scene: A broker opens a second location across town and staffs it with two associates. She never registers it because it's the same company. That's an unregistered branch office.
cards.trap: "It's the same company" sounds like a reason not to register. Same company is exactly why it's a branch. The real exception is narrow: a temporary on-site shelter used only for that subdivision's sales.
cards.remember: Every extra location is a branch, except the subdivision-only sales shelter.

question.q: A broker opens a second location across town, staffs it with two sales associates, and does not register it because "it's the same company." What is the correct view?
options: It is a branch office and must be registered separately, with its own fee and sign
The main office registration covers every location of the same company
It needs registration only if a broker works there full time
It needs its own sign, but not its own registration
question.why: Any additional location where the brokerage does business is a branch office, each registered separately with its own fee and sign. Being the same company is exactly why it is a branch, not a reason to skip registration.

cards.idea: Every ad by the brokerage or its associates must show the registered brokerage name where a reader can actually see it. Leave it out and it's a blind ad, which is prohibited. Online, that means every page and post.
cards.scene: A yard-sign rider on Bayshore Lane reads "The Rivera Group, call Daniel" with a cell number and nothing else. No brokerage name, so it's a blind ad, and the broker answers for it.
cards.trap: Thinking personal branding is the problem. It isn't. An associate or team name is allowed alongside the brokerage name, never instead of it. The broker is responsible even for an ad they never saw.
cards.remember: Brokerage name on every ad, every page, every post.

question.q: A yard-sign rider on Bayshore Lane shows a team name, "call" and a cell number, and nothing else. How does Florida treat it?
options: Allowed, because team names are permitted in advertising
A blind ad, because the brokerage's registered name is missing
Allowed, because the cell number lets the public reach a licensee
Allowed, as long as the broker approved the rider in advance
question.why: Every ad must show the brokerage's registered name where a reader can see it; without it the ad is blind and prohibited. Team names are allowed, which is the trap, but only alongside the brokerage name, never instead of it.

cards.idea: An associate delivers a deposit to the broker by the end of the next business day. The broker places it in escrow by the end of the third business day after the brokerage received it, at a Florida depository.
cards.scene: A buyer hands an associate a deposit on Friday evening. It's received Friday. The associate must get it to the broker by Monday. The broker must place it in escrow by Wednesday.
cards.trap: Business days, not calendar days. The exam offers the calendar-day answer and hopes you take it. And "received" means the day the associate got it, not the day it reached the broker's desk.
cards.remember: Associate: next business day. Broker: third business day after receipt.

question.q: A buyer hands a sales associate a deposit on Friday evening. By when must the associate deliver it to the broker?
options: By the end of Saturday
By the end of Monday
Before leaving the office Friday evening
By the end of Wednesday
question.why: The associate must deliver it by the end of the next business day, and the next business day after Friday is Monday. Saturday is the calendar-day answer the exam hopes you take.

cards.idea: Commingling is mixing escrow money with the brokerage's own. Conversion is using escrow money as your own. For bank charges, a broker may keep up to $1,000 of their own in sales escrow, $5,000 in property-management escrow.
cards.scene: A broker keeps $1,000 of her own money in the sales escrow account to cover bank charges. That's allowed. Using escrow to cover her payroll would be conversion, however quickly she paid it back.
cards.trap: A broker "borrows" $4,000 from escrow on Tuesday and returns it Friday. The bait is intent to repay. It isn't a defense: it was conversion the moment the money left.
cards.remember: Escrow money is never yours to borrow, even briefly.

question.q: A broker short on payroll takes $4,000 from the escrow account on Tuesday and puts it all back on Friday. What is this?
options: Conversion, from the moment the money left the account
Commingling, the lesser offense, because it was repaid
No violation, because it was repaid within the week
Permitted, because it is under the $5,000 property-management cushion
question.why: Using escrow money as your own is conversion, and intent to repay is not a defense. The $5,000 figure is a cushion of the broker's own money for bank charges, not a borrowing limit.

cards.idea: Once a month the broker writes a reconciliation of every escrow account: the bank balance, outstanding items, and the total of all individual deposits. Then signs, dates and keeps it. Shortages and overages get explained and corrected.
cards.scene: A broker files every monthly bank statement neatly but never writes the comparison against the deposits she holds. However tidy the binder, she hasn't reconciled anything.
cards.trap: Treating the bank statement as the reconciliation. It isn't one. Without a written comparison, signed and dated, the broker hasn't reconciled.
cards.remember: Monthly, written, signed, dated. A bank statement isn't a reconciliation.

question.q: Every month a broker files the escrow bank statements in a binder, but never writes any comparison. Has the broker reconciled the accounts?
options: Yes, the bank statement shows the account balance
Yes, if the bank has certified the statements
Yes, if the broker reviews the binder once a quarter
No, the bank statement is not the reconciliation
question.why: The reconciliation is the broker's own written comparison, prepared monthly, signed, dated and kept. Filing statements feels like recordkeeping, but a broker who never writes the comparison has not reconciled anything.

cards.idea: When both sides claim a deposit, or the broker has good-faith doubt, the broker may not decide. Notify FREC in writing within 15 business days of the last demand, then start a settlement procedure within 30 business days.
cards.scene: Buyer and seller both claim a deposit on Heron Bay Drive. The broker sits on it for a year with no notice and no procedure. That's the violation, whoever deserved the money.
cards.trap: Sitting on it. The four procedures are mediation, arbitration, litigation including interpleader, or a FREC escrow disbursement order. And a broker who obeys an EDO and is sued anyway is protected; FREC backs him.
cards.remember: Don't judge. Notify FREC within 15 business days; start a procedure within 30.

question.q: A buyer and seller on Heron Bay Drive both claim a deposit. The broker sends no notice, starts no procedure, and leaves it in escrow for a year. Later the seller turns out to be entitled. Is there a violation?
options: Yes, sitting on it without notice or a procedure is the violation
No, because the money stayed safely in escrow
No, because the rightful party is eventually paid
Only if the broker had a personal interest in the deal
question.why: Doing nothing is the violation, regardless of who deserved the money. Keeping funds safely in the account feels responsible, but the broker must notify FREC and start an authorized settlement procedure.

cards.idea: Only the employing broker can pay a sales associate for brokerage work. Selling rental lists needs a written contract and a refund rule. Records are kept five years, longer if litigation is pending.
cards.scene: At closing, a grateful seller hands the associate a thank-you check. A cooperating broker pays her directly to save a step. Both are violations. The money has to go through her employing broker.
cards.trap: Gratitude and convenience as excuses for direct payment. Neither works. On rental lists: no rental found within 30 days gets 75 percent back on request; an inaccurate list gets 100 percent.
cards.remember: Associates are paid only by their employing broker.

question.q: At closing, a grateful seller hands the sales associate a personal thank-you check. What is the correct view?
options: Allowed, because a gift is not a commission
Allowed, if the associate tells the broker about it
A violation, because only the employing broker may pay a sales associate
Allowed, if the seller is not the associate's client
question.why: Only the employing broker can pay a sales associate for brokerage work, so a seller's thank-you check is a violation. Calling it a gift or disclosing it does not change who is paying.

6.name: Violations of License Law, Penalties and Procedures

cards.idea: Complaint to DBPR, investigation, probable cause panel, formal complaint, then an informal hearing if the facts aren't disputed or a formal hearing before an administrative law judge. FREC issues the final order. Appeals go to a District Court of Appeal.
cards.scene: A seller complains to DBPR that a licensee kept her deposit. That's legally sufficient. After the investigation, the probable cause panel finds enough to proceed. A formal complaint follows, and the licensee, disputing the facts, gets a formal hearing.
cards.trap: Swapping the probable cause panel and the hearing. Probable cause comes before the formal complaint, not after. And the administrative law judge only recommends an order; FREC decides.
cards.remember: Probable cause before formal complaint. Judge recommends, FREC decides.

question.q: A licensee disputes the facts and has a formal hearing before an administrative law judge. Who issues the final order?
options: The administrative law judge
FREC
The probable cause panel
The District Court of Appeal
question.why: The administrative law judge issues only a recommended order. FREC issues the final order and can accept, reject or modify the recommended penalty.

cards.idea: FREC can deny a license, reprimand, impose probation, fine up to $5,000 per count, suspend up to 10 years, or revoke. Revocation is permanent, unless it was for a purely clerical mistake, which is without prejudice.
cards.scene: A licensee gets a citation, a fixed fine for a listed minor offense, and ignores it. After 30 days of doing nothing, she has accepted it. A notice of noncompliance would instead have given her a deadline to fix things.
cards.trap: The answer choice saying FREC can revoke only through a court. FREC revokes on its own authority; courts are for appeal. Keep the maximums straight too: $5,000 per count, suspension up to 10 years.
cards.remember: FREC revokes on its own authority. Courts only hear appeals.

question.q: FREC concludes a licensee's violation warrants revocation. What does FREC need in order to revoke the license?
options: A circuit court order confirming the revocation
A ruling from a District Court of Appeal
Nothing more, since FREC revokes on its own authority
The licensee's written agreement to the revocation
question.why: FREC revokes licenses on its own authority through its final order. Courts come in only if the licensee appeals.

cards.idea: Most license law violations are second-degree misdemeanors. The big exception is worse: operating without a license is a third-degree felony.
cards.scene: Someone with no license operates as a real estate licensee: a third-degree felony. A licensed associate who skips the required brokerage relationship disclosure has committed a license-law violation, but not a crime by itself.
cards.trap: The exam asks about failing to give the required brokerage relationship disclosures and hopes you call it a crime. It's a license-law violation, not a crime by itself. The felony is operating without a license.
cards.remember: Unlicensed activity: third-degree felony. Most other violations: second-degree misdemeanors.

question.q: Which of these is a third-degree felony?
options: Failing to give a required brokerage relationship disclosure
Running an ad without the brokerage name
Failing to prepare a monthly escrow reconciliation
Operating without a license
question.why: Operating without a license is the third-degree felony, while most license law violations are second-degree misdemeanors. Skipping a required disclosure is a license-law violation, not a crime by itself.

cards.idea: The exam uses this vocabulary precisely. Fraud is intentional deception. Misrepresentation is a false statement of fact, even an innocent one, that someone relied on. Concealment is hiding what you had a duty to disclose.
cards.scene: A sales associate's broker is suspended. The associate did nothing wrong and keeps the license, but it's ineffective: she can't work until she moves to a new broker. Not revoked, not void.
cards.trap: Calling that associate's license void or revoked. It's ineffective. Void means it never existed or has been revoked; involuntarily inactive means it lapsed because the licensee didn't renew.
cards.remember: Broker suspended: the associate's license is ineffective, not void.

question.q: A sales associate's employing broker has his license suspended. The associate did nothing wrong. What is the status of the associate's license?
options: Ineffective until she moves to a new broker
Void
Revoked along with the broker's
Involuntarily inactive
question.why: An ineffective license exists but can't be used, and she can work again once she moves to a new broker. Void means the license never existed or has been revoked.

cards.idea: Funded by licensee fees, it reimburses a member of the public harmed by a licensee's act who can't collect, after winning a judgment or arbitration award. It pays up to $50,000 per transaction, $150,000 total per licensee.
cards.scene: A buyer wins a judgment against a licensee and can't collect, so the fund pays her. That licensee's license is automatically suspended until the fund is repaid in full, with interest.
cards.trap: The exam swaps the two numbers. $50,000 is per transaction; $150,000 is the cap against any one licensee, however many claims. Also: a broker cheated by his own associate can't claim. The fund is for the public.
cards.remember: $50,000 per transaction, $150,000 per licensee. Never swap them.

question.q: Buyers in several separate transactions win uncollectible judgments against the same licensee. What is the most the Recovery Fund will pay in total on that licensee's account?
options: $50,000 for each claimant, with no total cap
Only the first claim filed is paid
question.why: The fund pays up to $50,000 per transaction but no more than $150,000 total against any one licensee, no matter how many claims.

7.name: Federal and State Laws Pertaining to Real Estate

cards.idea: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 bans race discrimination in any property transaction, with no exemptions. The Fair Housing Act of 1968 covers housing and seven protected classes. Florida's Fair Housing Act mirrors the federal list.
cards.scene: A landlord turns away a pregnant woman. That's familial status, which covers households with children under 18, pregnant women, and people getting custody. It's one of the seven federal classes.
cards.trap: Mixing up which law is which. Race falls under the 1866 Act, which has no exemptions. The seven federal classes are the exam's list; local ordinances may add more, but the exam doesn't test those.
cards.remember: 1866: race, no exemptions. 1968: seven classes, in housing.

question.q: Which of these is NOT one of the seven protected classes under the federal Fair Housing Act?
options: Familial status
Religion
Marital status
Handicap
question.why: The federal list is race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status and handicap. Local ordinances may add classes, but the federal list is the exam's list.

items.title: The exemptions, and why race is never one

cards.idea: The Fair Housing Act exempts some owners: no more than three single-family homes, sold without a broker or discriminatory ads; owner-occupied buildings of four units or fewer; religious organizations and private clubs; qualifying older-persons housing.
cards.scene: An owner lives in one unit of a four-unit building and rents the others herself. The Mrs. Murphy exemption may apply. The moment a broker is involved, it's gone. And it never covers refusing someone over race.
cards.trap: Using an exemption to excuse race discrimination. The 1866 Act has no exemptions, so none of them reach race. And none of them survive a licensee's involvement.
cards.remember: No exemption covers race, and none survives a licensee's involvement.

question.q: An owner-occupant of a four-unit building rents units herself, with no broker and no ads, and turns away an applicant because of his race. Is this lawful?
options: No, because the 1866 Civil Rights Act bans race discrimination with no exemptions
Yes, because the Mrs. Murphy exemption covers her
Yes, because no licensee was involved
Only if she lives in the building full time
question.why: The Mrs. Murphy exemption comes from the Fair Housing Act. The 1866 Act bans race discrimination in any property transaction and has no exemptions at all.

cards.idea: Steering guides buyers toward or away from areas by protected class. Blockbusting pushes owners to sell by suggesting a protected class is moving in. Redlining refuses loans or insurance by area. Discriminatory ads state or imply a preference.
cards.scene: A licensee on Coral Way shows a family with three children only the houses near the elementary school, because "that's what they'll want." That's steering on familial status.
cards.trap: Steering by good intentions. The exam makes the licensee helpful and hopes you call it good service. Helpful is not a defense. Let the buyer tell you what they want.
cards.remember: Good intentions don't excuse steering. Let the buyer choose.

question.q: A licensee shows a family with three children only homes near the elementary school, assuming that's what they'll want. What is this?
options: Good service, since it matches their likely needs
Blockbusting
Redlining
Steering on familial status
question.why: Guiding buyers toward or away from areas based on a protected class is steering, and helpful intent is no defense. Familial status is a protected class.

cards.idea: A fair housing complaint goes to HUD within one year, or to federal court as a civil action within two years. HUD investigates and tries conciliation. Florida complaints can also go to the Florida Commission on Human Relations.
cards.scene: A broker doesn't display the fair housing poster in her office. That alone isn't a violation. But if a complaint is filed against her, the missing poster is treated as evidence.
cards.trap: Mixing up the deadlines: one year to complain to HUD, two years for a federal civil action. And a missing poster is evidence in a complaint, not a violation by itself.
cards.remember: HUD within one year; federal court within two.

question.q: A renter believes she was turned away because of her religion. How long does she have to file a complaint with HUD?
options: Two years, the same as a federal lawsuit
One year
There is no deadline for a HUD complaint
Only until the unit is rented to someone else
question.why: A HUD complaint must be filed within one year. Two years is the deadline for a civil action in federal court.

cards.idea: The ADA isn't about housing. It covers public accommodations and commercial facilities, like a brokerage office, a store or a hotel. Barriers come out where readily achievable, and new construction and alterations must be accessible.
cards.scene: A licensee leases a store to a new tenant. That commercial property carries ADA obligations the tenant needs to know about. Her own brokerage office is a public accommodation too.
cards.trap: Confusing the ADA with the handicap provisions of fair housing. Keep them apart: housing is fair housing, businesses are ADA.
cards.remember: Housing is fair housing. Businesses are ADA.

question.q: A tenant with a disability asks his landlord to let him install grab bars in his apartment. Which law governs the request?
options: The Americans with Disabilities Act
The Civil Rights Act of 1866
The Fair Housing Act
Neither, because apartments are exempt
question.why: Housing falls under fair housing, not the ADA. The ADA covers public accommodations and commercial facilities, such as a brokerage office or a store.

items.title: Florida Residential Landlord and Tenant Act

cards.idea: Chapter 83, Part II, of the Florida Statutes governs residential tenancies. The landlord holds deposits in a Florida account or posts a bond, and tells the tenant in writing where it's held and whether it earns interest.
cards.scene: A tenant moves out. With no claim, the landlord returns the deposit within 15 days. To keep some, she sends written notice within 30 days, and the tenant has 15 days to object. Unpaid rent gets a three-day notice.
cards.trap: The exam offers "30 days to return the deposit." It's 15 to return, 30 to claim, 15 to object. Miss the 30-day notice and the landlord forfeits the right to keep any of it.
cards.remember: 15 to return, 30 to claim, 15 to object.

question.q: A tenant moves out and the landlord has no claim against the security deposit. How long does the landlord have to return it?
options: 15 days
30 days
Three days, not counting weekends and legal holidays
Seven days
question.why: With no claim, the deposit goes back within 15 days. Thirty days is the deadline for written notice of intent to keep some or all of it.

items.title: Land sales, telemarketing and the rest

cards.idea: The federal Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act makes a developer selling or leasing 25 or more unimproved lots across state lines register and give each buyer a property report. Do-Not-Call, CAN-SPAM and Junk Fax rules govern prospecting.
cards.scene: A licensee calls the owner of a just-expired listing on Palmetto Lane. The number is on the Do-Not-Call registry, and the old listing was with another brokerage. No existing business relationship, so the call is a violation.
cards.trap: Treating an expired listing, or "I was calling about a listing, not selling," as an exception. Neither is. The exception is an existing business relationship with this licensee, and there isn't one.
cards.remember: Check the Do-Not-Call registry before any cold call.

question.q: A licensee cold-calls the owner of a just-expired listing that was held by another brokerage. The owner's number is on the Do-Not-Call registry. What is the status of the call?
options: Allowed, because the property was recently listed for sale
Allowed, because the licensee was calling about a listing, not selling
Allowed, because expired listings are public information
A violation, because there is no existing business relationship
question.why: The registry exception is an existing business relationship, and the old listing was with a different brokerage. Calling about a listing is not an exception.

8.name: Property Rights: Estates and Tenancies; Condos, Co-ops, CDDs, HOAs, Time-Sharing

items.title: Real property, personal property and fixtures

cards.idea: Real property is land, what's permanently attached to it, and the rights that come with it. Personal property moves. A fixture started as personal property and became real by being attached. An agreement between the parties beats every other test.
cards.scene: A seller on Mango Street pulls the ceiling fans and the built-in bookcase before closing. "I bought them." Once wired and built in, they were part of the house. Unless the contract excluded them, they belonged to the buyer.
cards.trap: The exam dangles "she paid for them, so she keeps them." Wrong once they're attached. The flip side: a restaurant tenant's walk-in cooler is a trade fixture. The tenant takes it, not the landlord.
cards.remember: Attached means it stays, unless the contract says otherwise or it's a trade fixture.

question.q: A restaurant tenant installed a walk-in cooler for its business. The lease is ending. Who gets the cooler?
options: The tenant, who may remove it and must repair the damage
