The landlord, because anything attached becomes real property
The landlord, unless the lease says the tenant keeps it
Whoever paid more toward the installation
question.why: Equipment a commercial tenant installs for its business is a trade fixture and stays the tenant's personal property. The tenant can remove it before the lease ends, as long as it repairs the damage.

cards.idea: Ownership is a bundle of separate rights: to possess, use, enjoy, exclude and dispose. An owner can hand out single sticks, like a lease or an easement, and still own the property. Government keeps certain rights over all of it.
cards.scene: A landlord leases out a duplex on Tamarind Avenue. The tenant gets possession for the lease term. The landlord keeps everything else in the bundle, and possession comes back when the lease ends.
cards.trap: The exam suggests that leasing means the landlord "gave up ownership." Wrong. The landlord gave away one stick, possession, for a time, and still owns the property.
cards.remember: A lease or easement gives away a stick, not the bundle.

question.q: An owner leases her duplex on Tamarind Avenue to a tenant. During the lease, what does she hold?
options: Nothing, until the tenant moves out
Only the right to collect rent
The bundle of rights minus possession
A life estate lasting the lease term
question.why: A lease hands out one stick, possession, for a time. The landlord still owns the property and gets possession back when the lease ends.

cards.idea: Riparian rights go with land on a river or stream. Littoral rights go with a lake, sea or ocean. In Florida, land below the mean high-water line of navigable waters is generally state-owned and held in trust for the public.
cards.scene: An owner whose lot fronts the ocean owns down to the mean high-water line, not into the water. The public can use the wet sand below it. Her rights are littoral, because the ocean isn't a flowing river.
cards.trap: The exam offers "riparian" for an ocean or lake lot. Match the word to the water: river or stream is riparian; lake, sea or ocean is littoral. Both words will be on the page.
cards.remember: River or stream is riparian. Lake, sea or ocean is littoral.

question.q: An owner's lot fronts a lake. Which term describes her water rights?
options: Riparian rights
Littoral rights
Appurtenant rights
Easement rights
question.why: Lakes, seas and oceans carry littoral rights. Riparian rights belong to land along flowing water, a river or stream.

cards.idea: Fee simple absolute is the biggest estate: no time limit, no conditions, sellable and inheritable. A defeasible fee can be lost if a condition is broken. The deed's wording decides whether that loss is automatic.
cards.scene: A donor deeds a lot on Seagrape Circle to a church "so long as it is used for worship." The church turns it into a parking lot. Title is already back with the donor's heirs, no lawsuit needed.
cards.trap: The exam swaps the wording. "So long as," "while" or "during" is determinable and ends automatically. "On the condition that" or "provided that" is condition subsequent, and the heirs must act to re-enter.
cards.remember: "So long as" ends on its own. "On the condition that" needs action.

question.q: A lot on Seagrape Circle is deeded to a church "on the condition that" it be used for worship. The church builds a parking lot on it. What happens?
options: Title reverts to the grantor's heirs automatically
The church keeps it, because the condition is unenforceable
The grantor's heirs have a right of re-entry and must act to take it back
The state takes title by escheat
question.why: "On the condition that" creates a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent, which doesn't end on its own. Automatic reversion comes with "so long as" language, the determinable fee.

cards.idea: A life estate lasts for a named person's life; pur autre vie is measured by someone else's life. When it ends, property going back to the grantor is a reversion. Property going on to a third person is a remainder.
cards.scene: A life tenant on Cypress Hollow Road leases the farm for ten years, then dies in year three. The lease ends with her life estate. A tenant can't hold more than the landlord had.
cards.trap: The exam offers "the lease runs its full term." It doesn't; it ends with the life estate. It also swaps the future interests: back to the grantor is reversion, on to someone else is remainder.
cards.remember: Back to the grantor is reversion. On to someone else is remainder.

question.q: A grantor deeds a house to Rosa for life, then to Rosa's nephew. What does the nephew hold?
options: A reversion
A life estate pur autre vie
A tenancy in common with Rosa
A remainder
question.why: Property that passes to a third person named in the deed when a life estate ends is a remainder. A reversion is when it goes back to the original grantor.

cards.idea: A leasehold is the right to possess someone else's property for a time. An estate for years has fixed dates. A periodic tenancy renews until notice. A tenancy at will ends when either side chooses. Sufferance is an unconsented holdover.
cards.scene: A lease on Mango Street runs from February 1 to July 31. Six months, fixed dates. It's an estate for years, and it ends on July 31 with no notice required.
cards.trap: The exam bets you'll read "years" literally and reject a six-month lease. The test is fixed dates, not length. Also tested: death ends a tenancy at will, but not an estate for years or periodic tenancy.
cards.remember: Fixed start and end dates make an estate for years, whatever the length.

question.q: A lease on Mango Street runs from February 1 to July 31. What kind of tenancy is it?
options: Periodic tenancy
Estate for years
Tenancy at will
Tenancy at sufferance
question.why: Definite beginning and end dates make it an estate for years, even though it lasts six months. It ends on its end date without notice.

items.title: Forms of ownership: severalty and co-ownership

cards.idea: Severalty is one owner. Tenants in common share undivided interests with no survivorship. Florida doesn't presume survivorship: a deed to two people is a tenancy in common unless it expressly says otherwise. Married couples are presumed tenants by the entireties.
cards.scene: Two unmarried partners buy a condo on Tamarind Avenue. The deed names both and says nothing more. One dies. Her half goes to her heirs, not her partner, because they were tenants in common.
cards.trap: The exam assumes co-owners get survivorship. Not in Florida unless the deed expressly says so; "as joint tenants" alone may not be enough. Give a married couple the same deed and the survivor takes it all.
cards.remember: Florida presumes no survivorship, except for married couples.

question.q: Alma and Teo, who are not married, take a deed "to Alma and Teo" with no other language. Teo dies. Who gets his share?
options: Alma, by right of survivorship
Alma, as tenant by the entireties
The state, by escheat
Teo's heirs or devisees
question.why: Under section 689.15, a conveyance to two or more people is a tenancy in common unless it expressly provides for survivorship. A tenant in common's share passes to heirs or devisees.

items.title: Ownership by business entities and trusts

cards.idea: Property can be held by a corporation, partnership, LLC or trust. In a Florida land trust, a trustee holds legal title while beneficiaries control the property and its income, treated as personal property. The draws are privacy and easy transfers.
cards.scene: A deed on Seagrape Circle names a trustee as grantee, so the public record shows the trustee's name. The beneficiaries, named in the trust document, are the ones who actually control the house.
cards.trap: The exam suggests the trustee named on the deed personally owns the house. The trustee holds title for the beneficiaries, and the trust document says who controls it.
cards.remember: The trustee holds title. The beneficiaries hold control and income.

question.q: A house on Seagrape Circle is held in a Florida land trust. Who holds the rights to use and control it and to its income?
options: The beneficiaries
The trustee, as the title holder
The county, until the trust document is recorded
The original grantor
question.why: In a land trust the trustee holds legal title, but the beneficiaries hold the rights to use, control and income. The public record shows only the trustee's name.

cards.idea: Florida homestead does three separate things. It shields the home from most creditors. It restricts selling, mortgaging or leaving it by will. And it gives a property tax exemption. The exam keeps the three apart, and so should you.
cards.scene: A husband on Cypress Hollow Road owns the homestead in his own name from before the marriage. To sell it, he still needs his wife to join the deed, even though she isn't on title.
cards.trap: The exam blends the three. The half-acre and 160-acre limits are creditor protection, not the tax exemption. The $25,000 is the tax exemption, not creditor protection. A spouse must join even when off title.
cards.remember: Acreage limits stop creditors. $25,000 is tax. A spouse joins any sale.

question.q: A Florida resident's homestead sits on contiguous land outside a municipality. What does the 160-acre figure govern?
options: The land eligible for the $25,000 tax exemption
The cap on yearly Save Our Homes increases
The land protected from forced sale by most creditors
The land a spouse must approve before a sale
question.why: The half-acre and 160-acre limits define how much land is protected from forced sale. The $25,000 exemption is a separate tax benefit.

cards.idea: A condominium is a form of ownership, not a type of building. Each owner holds fee simple title to a unit plus an undivided interest in the common elements. Recording a declaration of condominium creates it.
cards.scene: A buyer signs a developer's contract for a new condo, then gets the last required document a week later. Her 15-day window runs from that later date. A resale buyer gets 7 days, excluding weekends and legal holidays.
cards.trap: The exam swaps the periods. Developer sale: 15 days. Resale: 7 days excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays; older printings say three. And a condo owner owns her unit, not a share in the building.
cards.remember: Condo cancel: 15 days from developer, 7 excluding weekends and holidays on resale.

question.q: A buyer signs a contract for a resale condo on Mango Street. Under the current statute, how long does she have to cancel?
options: 15 days after the later of signing or receiving the documents
7 days, excluding weekends and legal holidays, after the later of the two
3 days after the later of the two
7 calendar days, weekends included, after the later of the two
question.why: Section 718.503, as amended effective July 1, 2025, gives a resale buyer 7 days excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. Fifteen days is the developer-sale period, and three is the old version.

cards.idea: In a co-op, a corporation owns the building. Residents own shares of stock plus a proprietary lease on their unit, so the interest has historically been personal property. Florida treats it as real property for some purposes, including homestead.
cards.scene: A co-op shareholder pays her part of the building's single tax bill and its underlying mortgage. When enough neighbors stop paying, the remaining shareholders can be left covering the shortfall.
cards.trap: The exam mixes up co-op and condo. A deed to a unit with its own tax bill is a condo. Shares plus a proprietary lease and a shared building mortgage is a co-op.
cards.remember: Co-op: shares and a lease. Condo: a deed to the unit.

question.q: A buyer acquires shares in a corporation that owns a building, plus a proprietary lease on one unit. What does she own?
options: A cooperative interest
A condominium unit
A timeshare estate
A tenancy at will
question.why: Stock plus a proprietary lease is a co-op. A condo owner holds fee simple title to the unit itself, with its own tax bill.

cards.idea: A CDD is a special-purpose local government under Chapter 190. It issues bonds to build infrastructure like roads, water, sewer and drainage. Owners repay them through assessments on the property tax bill, often for many years.
cards.scene: A buyer in a new subdivision off Seagrape Circle opens a tax bill well above what the price suggests. The extra is the CDD assessment, and it's a lien on the property just like property taxes.
cards.trap: The exam calls a CDD an HOA. A CDD is local government, with an elected board and public meetings. An HOA is a private corporation under Chapter 720, and it handles paint and fence rules.
cards.remember: A CDD is government, and its assessments ride the tax bill as a lien.

question.q: A buyer off Seagrape Circle finds an extra assessment for roads and drainage on her property tax bill. What is its likely source?
options: The homeowners' association under Chapter 720
The condominium association
A Community Development District under Chapter 190
The county property appraiser's homestead office
question.why: A CDD is a special-purpose local government that repays infrastructure bonds through assessments on the property tax bill. An HOA is a private corporation that enforces deed restrictions.

cards.idea: An HOA governs separately owned homes. Each owner owns the lot and house; the association owns common areas and enforces deed restrictions. Membership is mandatory, and it can lien for unpaid assessments. Buyers get a disclosure summary under section 720.401.
cards.scene: A buyer signs for a house in a mandatory-HOA community, and the contract doesn't reference the disclosure summary. She gets the summary two days later. She can void within 3 days of receiving it, unless closing comes first.
cards.trap: The exam has the buyer sign, get the summary, close, then try to cancel two weeks later. Too late: the right lasts 3 days after receiving the summary or until closing, whichever comes first.
cards.remember: Missing HOA summary: void within 3 days or before closing, whichever comes first.

question.q: A contract for a house in a mandatory HOA community doesn't reference the disclosure summary. The buyer receives it, closes, and two weeks later wants out. Can she void the contract?
options: Yes, because the 3 days start at closing
No, the right ended at closing
Yes, any time before her first assessment is due
Yes, because the summary came after she signed
question.why: Under section 720.401 she could void within 3 days after receiving the summary or before closing, whichever came first. Closing ended the right.

cards.idea: A timeshare splits use of a resort unit into time periods sold to different buyers. A timeshare estate is a deeded ownership interest, so it's real property. A timeshare license is a contractual right to use, so it's personal property.
cards.scene: A buyer signs at a resort on Tamarind Avenue on a Saturday and receives every required document that day. She can cancel until midnight on the Tuesday ten days later, both weekends included.
cards.trap: The exam swaps in business days or the condo's 15. Under section 721.10 it's midnight of the 10th calendar day after the later of signing or the last document. The buyer can't waive it.
cards.remember: Timeshare: 10 calendar days, weekends counted, and it can't be waived.

question.q: A buyer signs a timeshare contract at a resort on Tamarind Avenue on a Saturday and gets all required documents that day. When does her cancellation right end?
options: Midnight on the 10th business day after signing
15 days after signing
Midnight on the following Saturday
Midnight on the Tuesday ten days later
question.why: Section 721.10 runs the right until midnight of the 10th calendar day, weekends included. Business days and a 15-day period belong to other rules.

cards.idea: Title is ownership itself, not a piece of paper. A deed is the written instrument that moves title from grantor to grantee. Title can move without a deed, by inheritance or court order, and a deed moves nothing until delivered.
cards.scene: A seller on Banyan Terrace hands the buyer a signed deed in a sealed envelope: "Don't open it until I die." He kept control. There was no delivery, so title hasn't passed.
cards.trap: The exam treats signing, or holding the paper, as the transfer. Title passes only when the deed is genuinely handed over with intent to transfer. A signed deed the grantor still controls is just paper.
cards.remember: Title is ownership. A deed only moves it once delivered.

question.q: A seller on Banyan Terrace signs a deed, seals it in an envelope, and tells the buyer not to open it until the seller dies. Has title passed?
options: Yes, when the seller signed it
Yes, when the buyer took the envelope
No, the seller kept control, so there was no delivery
No, because the deed was not yet recorded
question.why: Delivery means handing over the deed with intent to transfer, and this seller kept control. Recording isn't what passes title; delivery and acceptance do.

cards.idea: Voluntary alienation is the owner's choice: a sale, gift or will. Involuntary alienation isn't: descent, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure, adverse possession, and natural forces like accretion, reliction, erosion and avulsion.
cards.scene: A hurricane rips away a strip of a waterfront lot overnight. That's avulsion. Florida generally leaves the boundary where it was before the storm, so the owner doesn't lose title to the washed-away strip.
cards.trap: The exam swaps erosion and avulsion. Gradual loss is erosion, and the boundary moves. Sudden loss, as from a hurricane, is avulsion, and the boundary generally stays put.
cards.remember: Gradual loss moves the line. Sudden loss doesn't.

question.q: A hurricane suddenly washes away part of a waterfront lot. Under Florida's general rule, what happens to the boundary?
options: It moves to the new waterline, by erosion
It stays where it was before the event
It moves to the new waterline, by reliction
The lost land escheats to the state
question.why: Sudden loss is avulsion, and Florida generally leaves the boundary where it was before the event. Erosion is gradual and does move the boundary.

cards.idea: Actual, open, hostile, exclusive and continuous possession of someone else's land for 7 years can earn title. With color of title, that's enough. Without it, Florida also requires a return filed with the property appraiser and the taxes paid.
cards.scene: A neighbor on Snook Creek Road fences in a strip of the vacant lot next door and mows it for eight years. He has no color of title and never paid taxes on the strip. His claim fails.
cards.trap: The exam wants 7 and hides the taxes. Without color of title, years alone fail; no return and tax payments, no claim. Government land can't be adversely possessed, and recording title takes a quiet-title suit.
cards.remember: Seven years, and without color of title, the possessor must pay the taxes.

question.q: A neighbor on Snook Creek Road has openly fenced and used part of the next lot for eight years, with no deed and no tax payments. What is the result?
options: He owns it, since the 7-year period has run
He gets a prescriptive easement instead
The claim fails without the tax payments
He owns it once he records a notice of his claim
question.why: Without color of title, Florida requires a return filed with the property appraiser and the property taxes paid during the 7 years. Time alone isn't enough.

items.title: What makes a Florida deed valid

cards.idea: A valid Florida deed needs writing, a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, words of conveyance, recited consideration, a legal description, the grantor's signature, two witnesses, and delivery and acceptance. A notary is needed only to record it.
cards.scene: A grantor signs a deed in front of a notary, who acknowledges it. No witnesses sign. In Florida the deed fails, because section 689.01 requires two subscribing witnesses. The buyer never signs either, and that part is fine.
cards.trap: The exam offers a notarized deed with no witnesses as valid. It isn't; the notary doesn't replace the two witnesses. And "invalid because the buyer never signed" is wrong. Only the grantor signs.
cards.remember: Two witnesses make it valid. A notary makes it recordable.

question.q: A grantor signs a deed before a notary, and no witnesses sign. The grantee does not sign. Is the deed valid in Florida?
options: No, it lacks two subscribing witnesses
Yes, the notary's acknowledgment is enough
No, because the grantee never signed
Yes, once it is recorded
question.why: Section 689.01 requires the grantor to sign in the presence of two subscribing witnesses. Acknowledgment is needed only to record, and the grantee never has to sign.

cards.idea: The premises hold the parties, consideration, granting words and legal description. The habendum, "to have and to hold," defines the estate. The testimonium closes with signatures. Exceptions and reservations list what the grantor keeps or the deed is subject to.
cards.scene: A deed's granting clause says "grants, bargains, sells and conveys." Its habendum clause says "to have and to hold" for the grantee's life. That second clause is what tells you the estate is a life estate.
cards.trap: The exam swaps the habendum and the granting clause. The granting clause transfers. The habendum clause describes the estate being granted, such as fee simple or a life estate.
cards.remember: The granting clause transfers. The habendum defines the estate.

question.q: Which part of a deed defines the estate being granted, such as fee simple or a life estate?
options: The granting clause
The testimonium clause
The exceptions and reservations
The habendum clause
question.why: The habendum, "to have and to hold," defines the estate. The granting clause holds the words that transfer it.

cards.idea: Deed types differ only in what the grantor promises about title. A general warranty covers all defects, even earlier ones. A special warranty covers only defects arising while the grantor owned it. A quitclaim promises nothing.
cards.scene: A bank sells a foreclosed house on Ixora Drive with a special warranty deed. A defect from the prior owner, who lost it in foreclosure, isn't covered; only defects the bank created are. Title insurance protects the buyer.
cards.trap: The exam suggests the bank's deed covers the old owner's defects. A special warranty covers only "by, through or under" the grantor. Also wrong: "a quitclaim can't pass full title." It does, if the grantor has it.
cards.remember: A special warranty covers only the grantor's own time as owner.

question.q: A buyer takes a bank-owned house on Ixora Drive by special warranty deed. A title defect from the owner before the bank surfaces. What protects the buyer?
options: The bank's warranty, since the bank is the seller
Title insurance, not the deed
The bank's covenant of further assurance
The foreclosure judgment against the prior owner
question.why: A special warranty deed covers only defects that arose while the grantor owned the property. The earlier owner's defect falls outside it, so title insurance is the buyer's protection.

cards.idea: Recording with the county Clerk of the Circuit Court gives the world constructive notice. It doesn't make a deed valid; delivery does. Florida is a notice state: a later buyer who pays value without notice beats an unrecorded earlier deed.
cards.scene: A seller on Wild Coffee Lane sells to Buyer A, who doesn't record, then sells again to Buyer B. B pays full price, knows nothing of A, and finds the house vacant. B wins under Florida's notice statute.
cards.trap: The exam flips one fact: A has moved in. Possession is notice, so B is charged with knowing, and A wins. Also wrong: "whoever records first wins." A buyer without notice can win while recording second.
cards.remember: A buyer for value without notice wins. Possession counts as notice.

question.q: A seller on Wild Coffee Lane sells to Buyer A, who moves in but never records. The seller then sells to Buyer B, who pays full price and records. Who has the better claim?
options: Buyer B, who recorded first
Buyer B, who paid full value
Neither, until a court divides the property
Buyer A, whose possession gave B notice
question.why: Florida's notice statute protects only a later buyer who paid value without notice. A's possession charged B with notice, so A wins.

cards.idea: Buyers prove title three ways: an abstract with an attorney's opinion, title insurance, or a certificate of title. Only title insurance is insurance. An owner's policy protects the buyer; a lender's policy protects only the lender.
cards.scene: A buyer on Snook Creek Road says, "The lender got title insurance, so I'm covered." She isn't. The lender's policy protects the lender, for the loan balance. Only an owner's policy protects her.
cards.trap: The exam offers the lender's policy as the buyer's protection. It isn't. Also tested: Florida's Marketable Record Title Act uses a 30-year root of title, and an abstract is a history, not a guarantee.
cards.remember: The lender's policy protects the lender. Only an owner's policy protects the buyer.

question.q: A buyer on Snook Creek Road finances her purchase, and her lender requires a lender's title policy. Whom does that policy protect?
options: Only the lender, for the loan balance
The buyer and the lender equally
The buyer, for the purchase price
The seller, who gave the deed's warranties
question.why: A lender's policy protects only the lender, and its coverage falls as the loan is paid down. The buyer needs her own owner's policy.

items.title: Ownership restrictions: the government's four powers

cards.idea: Every owner holds title subject to four government powers, PETE: police power, eminent domain, taxation and escheat. Only eminent domain, an actual taking, requires compensation, and Florida's constitution requires full compensation.
cards.scene: A county rezones a vacant lot, limiting what can be built and lowering its value. That's police power, and no compensation is owed. If the county took the lot outright for public use, it would owe full compensation.
cards.trap: The exam calls value-lowering zoning a taking and says the owner must be paid. Ordinary regulation is police power, with no compensation. Eminent domain is a taking, and compensation is owed.
cards.remember: PETE. Regulation owes nothing; a taking must be paid for.

question.q: A county rezones a lot, which lowers its market value. Which power is this, and is compensation owed?
options: Eminent domain, and full compensation is owed
Police power, and no compensation is owed
Taxation, and the owner gets a tax credit
Escheat, and the state pays the difference
question.why: Zoning is police power, and ordinary regulation owes no compensation. Compensation is owed only when government takes property through eminent domain.

cards.idea: A lien is a claim on property as security for a debt. Liens are voluntary or involuntary, specific or general. In Florida, property tax liens come ahead of almost every other lien, including mortgages recorded earlier.
cards.scene: A homeowner on Banyan Terrace pays her contractor in full for a kitchen remodel. He never pays the cabinet supplier. The supplier, having served its notice correctly, records a construction lien on her house anyway.
cards.trap: The exam says paying the general contractor in full ends the lien risk. It doesn't; subcontractors and suppliers keep their lien rights. A claim of lien must be recorded within 90 days after final furnishing.
cards.remember: Paying the contractor doesn't stop supplier liens. Collect lien releases first.

question.q: A homeowner on Banyan Terrace pays her general contractor in full. He never pays the cabinet supplier, who served its notice correctly. Can the supplier lien her house?
options: No, because she paid in full
No, only the general contractor can claim a lien
Yes, the supplier keeps its construction lien rights
Only if she signed a contract with the supplier
question.why: Under Florida's construction lien law, a supplier that served its notice correctly keeps lien rights even after the owner pays the contractor. That's why owners collect lien releases before final payment.

cards.idea: An easement is a right to use another's land without possessing it. Appurtenant easements tie a dominant parcel to a servient one and run with the land. Easements in gross, like utility lines, benefit a person or company.
cards.scene: A neighbor on Ixora Drive has walked across the back of the next lot to reach the canal for 10 years. That's not a prescriptive easement in Florida. The period is 20 years.
cards.trap: The exam treats the neighbor's 10 years as enough. Florida's prescriptive period is 20. And a landlocked lot gets an easement by necessity only if a common owner's split of the land caused it.
cards.remember: Prescriptive easement: 20 years, and a right to use, not ownership.

question.q: A neighbor on Ixora Drive has openly crossed the next lot to reach the canal, without permission, for 10 years. What does he have?
options: No easement yet, because Florida's prescriptive period is 20 years
A prescriptive easement
An easement by necessity
Ownership of the path he walks
question.why: Florida's prescriptive period is 20 years, so 10 years of use isn't enough. Even after 20, he would get a right to use, not ownership.

cards.idea: An encroachment physically intrudes onto someone else's land, like a fence or roof overhang, and a survey finds it, not a title search. Deed restrictions are private limits on use. When they conflict with zoning, the more restrictive one controls.
cards.scene: Zoning on Wild Coffee Lane allows a duplex. The subdivision's recorded covenants allow only single-family homes. An owner who wants to build a duplex can't, because the covenants are stricter and control.
cards.trap: The exam suggests zoning permission overrides a private restriction. It doesn't; the more restrictive rule wins, whichever it is. Restrictions that discriminate against a protected class are unenforceable, even if still printed.
cards.remember: Zoning versus covenant: the stricter one wins.

question.q: Zoning on Wild Coffee Lane allows duplexes, but the recorded subdivision covenants allow only single-family homes. Can an owner build a duplex?
options: Yes, because zoning overrides private covenants
No, because the more restrictive rule controls
Yes, if the county issues a building permit
Only after a quiet-title judgment
question.why: When a deed restriction and a zoning ordinance conflict, the more restrictive one controls. Zoning permission doesn't override the single-family covenant.

items.title: Why a street address is not enough

cards.idea: A legal description identifies one parcel and only one, with boundaries that can be found on the ground. A street address tells the mail carrier where to go. A parcel ID is a tax-roll reference. Neither is a legal description.
cards.scene: A contract for 2210 Spanish Moss Trail lists only the street address and the parcel ID. The contract can still be enforceable if the property can be identified. The deed at closing needs the full legal description.
cards.trap: Whenever the exam asks what a legal description is, "street address" and "tax parcel number" are the wrong answers it dangles. Streets get renamed, numbers get reassigned, and neither shows boundary lines.
cards.remember: An address finds the mailbox, not the boundaries.

question.q: Which of these is a legal description of a Florida parcel?
options: The street address, 2210 Spanish Moss Trail
The county parcel identification number
A description identifying one parcel with boundaries locatable on the ground
The owner's name and mailing address
question.why: A legal description must identify one parcel only, with boundaries that can be located on the ground. A street address and a parcel ID do neither.

cards.idea: Every calculation rests on a few numbers. A mile is 5,280 feet. An acre is 43,560 square feet. A section is one square mile, 640 acres. A township is 36 sections. An acre is area, not a shape.
cards.scene: A long, thin lot and a square one can each be exactly one acre, 43,560 square feet either way. A square acre is about 208.71 feet on a side, a number the exam uses more as a distractor than a tool.
cards.trap: The exam switches between linear and square units. An acre is 43,560 square feet; a mile is 5,280 feet in a straight line. A square mile is 640 acres, about 27.9 million square feet.
cards.remember: Acre: 43,560 square feet. Section: 640 acres. Mile: 5,280 feet.

question.q: How many square feet are in one acre?
question.why: An acre is 43,560 square feet. 5,280 is the feet in a mile, a linear measure, and 640 is the acres in a section.

cards.idea: Metes are distances and directions; bounds are the monuments the lines run between. A description starts at a point of beginning, runs courses and distances, and must return to that point. Monuments generally beat stated distances.
cards.scene: A waterfront parcel on Osprey Ridge Road starts at "the southwest corner of Section 14, thence North 300 feet to the point of beginning." The section corner is the point of commencement. The parcel starts 300 feet north.
cards.trap: The exam asks for the point of beginning and offers the section corner. That corner is where the surveyor started measuring, the point of commencement. The point of beginning is the parcel's own first corner.
cards.remember: Commencement starts the measuring. The point of beginning starts the parcel.

question.q: A description on Osprey Ridge Road runs from "the southwest corner of Section 14, thence North 300 feet to the point of beginning." Where is the point of beginning?
options: At the southwest corner of Section 14
At the center of Section 14
300 feet east of that corner
300 feet north of that corner
question.why: The section corner is the point of commencement, where the measuring starts. The parcel's first corner, the point of beginning, is 300 feet north of it.

cards.idea: The rectangular survey system grids land into squares counted from a principal meridian and a base line. Florida's starting point is the Tallahassee Meridian and its base line, which cross in Tallahassee.
cards.scene: A parcel in most of the peninsula is described as Township South, Range East, because most Florida land lies south and east of Tallahassee. Parts of the Panhandle west of Tallahassee are in ranges west.
cards.trap: The exam asks which principal meridian governs Florida land and dangles a federal meridian named for another state, or one through Miami. The answer is the Tallahassee Meridian.
cards.remember: Florida counts every township from the Tallahassee Meridian and base line.

question.q: Which principal meridian is the starting point for government survey descriptions in Florida?
options: A meridian passing through Miami
A federal meridian named for another state
The Tallahassee Meridian
The Florida-Georgia state line
question.why: Florida's grid starts where the Tallahassee Meridian and its base line intersect, in Tallahassee. Every Florida township is located by counting from that point.

cards.idea: Township lines run east–west every six miles from the base line. Range lines run north–south every six miles from the meridian. Where a row and a column cross, the six-by-six-mile square is also called a township: 36 square miles.
cards.scene: "Township 4 South, Range 3 East" names one square by its row and column: a row of townships south of the base line, a column of ranges east of the meridian. That square holds 36 square miles.
cards.trap: The exam leans on "township" meaning two things. Asked how many square miles are in a township, answer 36. Asked how far apart township lines are, answer 6 miles. Township lines run east–west.
cards.remember: Township lines are six miles apart; a township holds 36 square miles.

question.q: How far apart are township lines?
options: 36 miles
24 miles
1 mile
6 miles
question.why: Township lines run east–west every six miles. Thirty-six is the square miles in a township, and 24 miles is the spacing of the correction lines.

cards.idea: Each township holds 36 sections, each one mile square and 640 acres. Numbering starts with section 1 in the northeast corner, runs east to west, then snakes back and forth until section 36 in the southeast corner.
cards.scene: Draw it once. The top row runs right to left, 1 through 6. Section 7 sits under 6, and that row runs left to right to 12. Section 6 lands northwest, 31 southwest, 36 southeast.
cards.trap: The exam bets you'll start in the northwest, the way you read a page. It starts in the northeast. Expect "which section is in the northwest corner" (6) and "which is directly south of section 1" (12).
cards.remember: Section 1 is northeast. Snake back and forth to 36, southeast.

question.q: Which section lies directly south of section 1 in a township?
options: Section 2
Section 7
Section 12
Section 6
question.why: Section 1 is in the northeast corner, and the second row runs west to east from 7 to 12, putting 12 directly below 1. Section 7 sits under section 6, in the northwest.

cards.idea: Descriptions run from smallest piece to largest; locate by reading backward. For acreage, multiply the denominators and divide 640 by the result. "Of" means a piece inside the next piece. "And" joins separate pieces you add.
cards.scene: A buyer on Spanish Moss Trail gets "the E 1/2 of the SE 1/4": a strip 1,320 feet wide and 2,640 feet long. Fencing it is a perimeter question: 1,320 + 2,640 + 1,320 + 2,640 = 7,920 feet.
cards.trap: The exam puts "of" and "and" in one description. "The N 1/2 of the NE 1/4 and the SE 1/4 of the NE 1/4" is 80 plus 40: 120 acres. Multiply through the "and" and you land too small.
cards.remember: "Of" multiplies and shrinks. "And" adds separate pieces.

question.q: How many acres are in "the N 1/2 of the NE 1/4 and the SE 1/4 of the NE 1/4 of Section 22"?
options: 120 acres
80 acres
40 acres
20 acres
question.why: "And" joins two separate pieces: the N 1/2 of the NE 1/4 is 80 acres and the SE 1/4 of the NE 1/4 is 40, for 120. Multiplying through the "and" would give a much smaller parcel.

cards.idea: Most Florida homes are described by lot and block. A surveyor's plat maps every lot, block, street and easement, and is recorded under Chapter 177. A description then needs the lot, block, subdivision, plat book and page, and county.
cards.scene: "Lot 14, Block C, of SILVER PALM ESTATES, according to the plat thereof recorded in Plat Book 112, Page 37, of the Public Records of Broward County, Florida." That one line brings in everything on the plat.
cards.trap: The exam offers "Lot 14, Block C, Silver Palm Estates" as complete. Without the plat book and page, it may not identify one parcel, say after a replat. The recording reference is what makes it a legal description.
cards.remember: Lot, block, subdivision, plat book and page, county. Drop the reference and it fails.

question.q: What is missing from "Lot 14, Block C, Silver Palm Estates, Broward County" that keeps it from being a reliable legal description?
options: The street address
The plat book and page where the plat is recorded
The parcel identification number
The owner's name
question.why: Lot and block works by reference to the recorded plat, so the plat book and page tie it to one parcel. Without them, a similar subdivision name or a replat can leave it ambiguous.

cards.idea: Ownership runs below the surface and up into the air, within reasonable limits. A high-floor condo unit needs a three-dimensional description, with floor and ceiling heights measured from a datum, an established elevation, through local benchmarks.
cards.scene: A 12th-floor condo on Magnolia Bend is described as Unit 1204 according to the recorded declaration of condominium. The declaration and its survey fix the unit's floor and ceiling heights, not just its footprint.
cards.trap: The exam treats a condo unit like a lot-and-block parcel and offers a plat reference. A condo unit is described by reference to the recorded declaration of condominium, not a plat.
cards.remember: Condo units point to the declaration, not a plat.

question.q: A condo unit on Magnolia Bend is legally described by reference to which recorded document?
options: The subdivision plat
The county tax roll
The building permit
The declaration of condominium
question.why: The declaration and its attached survey set each unit's horizontal and vertical boundaries, so the description cites the recorded declaration. A plat is the reference for lot and block.

cards.idea: A survey maps boundaries, improvements, encroachments and easements, and catches the neighbor's fence over the line that a title search misses. Area math is simple: rectangles are length times width, triangles base times height divided by two.
cards.scene: A lot on Osprey Ridge Road listed as "75 × 140" has 75 feet facing the road. A lot listed as 80 × 125, at a scenario $2,500 per front foot, costs 80 × $2,500, or $200,000.
cards.trap: Front footage is always the first number. The exam prices a lot by the front foot and hopes you'll multiply by depth instead. On "75 × 140," the frontage is 75 feet, not 140.
cards.remember: The first number is frontage. Front-foot prices use only that.

question.q: A lot on Osprey Ridge Road is listed as "75 × 140." How many feet of frontage does it have?
options: 75 feet
140 feet
Whichever side is longer
None until a survey states it
question.why: Front footage is always listed first, so the lot has 75 feet facing the road. The 140 feet is depth, which a front-foot price ignores.

items.title: What a contract is, and how contracts are classified

cards.idea: A contract is an agreement between competent parties, backed by consideration, to do something legal. The exam sorts contracts in pairs: express or implied, bilateral or unilateral, executed or executory. Know each pair cold.
cards.scene: Buyer and seller on Loquat Street both signed last week. Closing is next month. Until closing, that contract is executory: something is still left to do. The deed, once delivered, is the executed piece.
cards.trap: The exam leans on everyday English, where executed means signed. In contract law it means fully performed. A signed contract waiting on closing is executory, and executed is the wrong answer.
cards.remember: Executed means fully performed, not signed. Signed and waiting to close is executory.

question.q: Both parties signed a sales contract on Loquat Street last week. Closing is next month. How is the contract classified today?
options: Executed, because both parties have signed it
Executory, because performance is still pending
Unilateral, because only the seller is bound so far
Implied, because the deed has not been delivered
question.why: Executed means fully performed by everyone, and closing hasn't happened yet. Signing alone leaves the contract executory.

cards.idea: A valid contract needs competent parties, offer and acceptance, consideration, and a legal purpose. For real estate, add a writing signed by the party to be charged. Consideration is usually the price for the property.
cards.scene: A buyer on Mangrove Bend signs a sales contract and puts down no earnest money at all. The deal is still valid. The buyer's promise to pay and the seller's promise to sell are the consideration.
cards.trap: The exam suggests a contract with no deposit is invalid. Wrong. The deposit is evidence of seriousness and protects the seller. The mutual promises are the consideration that makes the deal.
cards.remember: No deposit needed. Mutual promises are the consideration.

question.q: A buyer on Mangrove Bend signs a sales contract with the seller but gives no earnest money deposit. What is the status of the contract?
options: Void, because there is no consideration
Voidable by the seller until a deposit is paid
Valid, because the mutual promises are consideration
Unenforceable until a deposit reaches the escrow agent
question.why: The exchange of promises is consideration, so the contract is valid without earnest money. The deposit shows seriousness and protects the seller; it doesn't create the deal.

cards.idea: Florida's statute of frauds, Section 725.01, says contracts to sell land and leases over one year must be written and signed by the party being held to them. Otherwise a court won't enforce them.
cards.scene: Seller and buyer on Hibiscus Avenue agree out loud on price and closing date, nothing in writing. The seller backs out. The buyer can't enforce it in court. Had they gone ahead and closed, the sale would be fine.
cards.trap: The exam offers void or illegal for the oral land deal. It is neither. It is unenforceable: valid if both perform voluntarily, but neither side can force the other. Leases of one year or less may be oral.
cards.remember: An oral land contract isn't void. It's unenforceable.

question.q: A seller on Hibiscus Avenue orally agrees with a buyer on price and closing date, then backs out. What is the oral agreement?
options: Void, because it was never a contract
Illegal, so both parties face penalties
Voidable at the buyer's option
Unenforceable under the statute of frauds
question.why: A contract to sell land must be in writing to be enforced in court, but the oral deal isn't void or illegal. Had both sides closed voluntarily, nothing would be wrong with the sale.

items.title: Offer, acceptance, and when the contract exists

cards.idea: A contract exists when the offeree accepts in writing, without changes, and that acceptance is communicated back to the offeror. Any change at all is a counteroffer, which kills the original offer and flips the roles.
cards.scene: The seller on Firebush Court signs the buyer's offer but moves closing back a week and initials it. No contract yet. Until the buyer initials and it's delivered back, the seller may take a better offer, and the buyer may walk.
cards.trap: The exam calls the seller's signed-but-changed offer an acceptance. Even a one-week date change is a counteroffer, and it rejects the original. Signing isn't enough either: acceptance must be communicated back.
cards.remember: Any change is a counteroffer. No contract until unchanged acceptance is communicated.

question.q: A seller on Firebush Court signs a buyer's offer but changes the closing date by one week and initials the change. What has the seller done?
options: Accepted the offer, with a minor amendment
Made a counteroffer that rejected the original offer
Created a contract effective on the seller's signature
Accepted the offer, subject to the buyer's later approval
question.why: Acceptance must match the offer exactly, so any change to any term is a counteroffer. There is no contract until the buyer accepts the change and it is delivered back.

cards.idea: Valid has every element. Void was never a contract, like one for an illegal purpose. Voidable is valid, but one party may cancel, such as a minor or a fraud victim. Unenforceable is valid, but courts won't enforce it.
cards.scene: An adult signs a contract with a 16-year-old on Poinsettia Drive. The minor can keep the deal or cancel it. The adult can't cancel and is stuck with whatever the minor decides.
cards.trap: The exam offers void for the contract with a minor. It is voidable, and only the minor may cancel. Void is for a missing essential element, like a legal purpose, and nobody can enforce it.
cards.remember: A minor's contract is voidable by the minor. An illegal purpose is void.

question.q: An adult signs a contract with a 16-year-old on Poinsettia Drive. How is the contract classified?
options: Void, so neither party can enforce it
Voidable, at the option of either party
Voidable, at the option of the minor only
Unenforceable, so a court will not hear it
question.why: A contract with a minor is voidable at the minor's option: the minor may keep it or cancel it. The adult has no right to cancel.

items.title: Licensees and the practice of law

cards.idea: Florida licensees may fill in the blanks on standard forms, mainly those approved by Florida Realtors and The Florida Bar. Drafting clauses from scratch or advising on their legal effect is the unauthorized practice of law.
cards.scene: A buyer on Loquat Street asks the associate to just add a paragraph letting him out if his business deal falls through. She can pick a pre-printed approved addendum. Beyond the forms, she recommends an attorney.
cards.trap: The exam treats a hand-written custom clause in the margin as fine because the client asked for it. It is the violation. Choosing an approved pre-printed addendum is allowed; writing new legal language is not.
cards.remember: Fill in approved forms. Never write new legal clauses. Refer to an attorney.

question.q: A buyer on Loquat Street asks the sales associate to add a clause letting him cancel if his business deal falls through. What may she do?
options: Write the clause in the margin, since the buyer requested it
Draft the clause, as long as the seller initials it too
Use an approved pre-printed addendum or recommend an attorney
Explain the clause's legal effect and let the buyer write it
question.why: Licensees may fill in approved standard forms but may not write custom legal clauses or give legal advice. When the forms don't cover it, the job is to recommend an attorney.

items.title: Listing agreements and buyer brokerage agreements

cards.idea: A listing hires the brokerage, and it belongs to the broker, not the associate. Under Section 475.25(1)(r), a written listing needs a definite expiration date, property description, price and terms, fee, and the principal's signature.
cards.scene: A listing on Mangrove Bend runs for 90 days and renews automatically each month until the seller cancels in writing. That renewal clause violates Florida law, because it forces the seller to give notice after expiration.
cards.trap: Automatic renewal sounds like normal business. Florida bars any clause requiring the owner to notify the broker after expiration. And the copy is due within 24 hours of obtaining the signed listing, not from business day's end.
cards.remember: Definite expiration date, no auto-renewal, copy to the principal within 24 hours.

question.q: A written listing on Mangrove Bend runs 90 days and then renews monthly until the seller cancels in writing. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing, as long as the seller initialed the renewal clause
Nothing, because the 90-day term is a definite expiration date
It requires the seller to give notice after the expiration date
The renewal is valid only if the broker also signs it
question.why: Florida forbids a listing provision requiring the owner to notify the broker of cancellation after the expiration date. An automatic renewal the owner must opt out of does exactly that.

items.title: The sales contract: the Florida Realtors/Florida Bar forms

cards.idea: Most Florida home sales use one of two FR/BAR forms. In the standard form the seller has repair obligations up to written limits. In the AS IS form the seller makes no repairs, but the buyer gets an inspection period.
cards.scene: A buyer under the AS IS form on Hibiscus Avenue gets a clean inspection but now dislikes the neighborhood. During the inspection period he can cancel in his sole discretion and get his deposit back. Afterward, that right is gone.
cards.trap: The exam suggests the AS IS buyer needs a defect to cancel. He doesn't; it's his sole discretion. What matters is the deadline, not the reason. Once the inspection period ends, so does the right.
cards.remember: AS IS inspection period: cancel for any reason, but only before it ends.

question.q: Under the FR/BAR AS IS contract, a buyer on Hibiscus Avenue gets a clean inspection but changes his mind about the neighborhood. Can he cancel and recover his deposit?
options: Yes, if he cancels within the inspection period
No, because the inspection found no defects
Yes, at any time before closing
No, because an AS IS buyer has no cancellation right
question.why: During the inspection period the AS IS buyer may cancel in his sole discretion and get the deposit back. Once the period ends, that right is gone.

cards.idea: Under Johnson v. Davis, a Florida residential seller must disclose known facts that materially affect value, aren't readily observable, and aren't known to the buyer. An as-is clause doesn't excuse it. Licensees have their own similar duty.
cards.scene: A seller on Firebush Court had the attic replaced after termite damage, then repainted, and says nothing because the contract is AS IS. That hides a known, material defect, and Johnson v. Davis required him to disclose it.
cards.trap: The exam suggests AS IS lets the seller stay quiet. It doesn't. AS IS protects the seller from repair demands, not from concealing a known, material defect the buyer can't see.
cards.remember: AS IS limits repairs, never the duty to disclose hidden defects.

question.q: A seller on Firebush Court had the attic replaced after termite damage, repainted, and sells under an AS IS contract without mentioning it. What is true?
options: The AS IS clause relieves the seller of any duty to disclose
The seller had a duty to disclose the known, hidden, material defect
Disclosure is required only if the buyer asks about it directly
Only the licensee, not the seller, has a duty to disclose
question.why: Under Johnson v. Davis, a residential seller must disclose known facts that materially affect value and aren't readily observable. AS IS protects against repair demands, not concealment.

items.title: Options and rights of first refusal

cards.idea: An option gives the optionee the right, not the duty, to buy at a set price and time. Until exercised it's unilateral, and the optionor can't revoke. A right of first refusal only lets the holder match another offer.
cards.scene: Two tenants on Poinsettia Drive. One holds an option at $410,000 and can force the sale at that price within the option period. The other holds a right of first refusal and must wait for the owner to get an offer.
cards.trap: The exam blurs the two. Only the option holder can force a sale. The right-of-first-refusal holder can do nothing until the owner receives an offer, and then can only match it. The owner needn't sell at all.
cards.remember: An option can force the sale. A first refusal can only match.

question.q: A tenant on Poinsettia Drive holds a right of first refusal, not an option. The owner hasn't received any offers. What can the tenant do?
options: Force a sale at the current market price
Exercise the right at any time during the lease
Buy at the price stated in the lease
Nothing until the owner receives an offer to match
question.why: A right of first refusal only lets the holder match an offer the owner receives, if the owner decides to sell. Forcing a sale at a set price is what an option does.

cards.idea: Under a contract for deed, the buyer takes possession and pays in installments, while the seller keeps legal title until the price, or an agreed portion, is paid. Florida courts generally treat buyer default much like a mortgage default.
cards.scene: A buyer on Loquat Street moves in under a contract for deed and pays the seller in installments. He holds equitable title and possession now. If he defaults, the seller usually has to go to court rather than simply retake the house.
cards.trap: The exam says the contract-for-deed buyer owns nothing until the last payment. Wrong. He holds equitable title and possession. The seller holds only legal title.
cards.remember: Contract for deed: buyer has equitable title and possession; seller keeps legal title.

question.q: A buyer on Loquat Street is making installment payments under a contract for deed. What does he hold before the final payment?
options: Equitable title and possession
Nothing until the deed is delivered
Legal title, with the seller holding a lien
A leasehold interest only
question.why: Under a contract for deed the buyer holds equitable title and possession while the seller keeps legal title. He owns more than nothing before the last payment.

cards.idea: Assignment transfers your contract rights, but you stay liable if the assignee doesn't perform. Novation replaces the contract or party and releases the original. Contracts end by performance, mutual agreement, impossibility, or operation of law.
cards.scene: A buyer on Mangrove Bend assigns her purchase contract to her cousin and thinks she's out of the deal. If the cousin fails to close, she's still liable. Only a novation would have released her.
cards.trap: The exam suggests assignment ends the original party's obligations. It doesn't; the assignor stays liable. Only novation releases the original party, as when a lender releases the original borrower on a loan assumption.
cards.remember: Assignment keeps you liable. Novation releases you.

question.q: A buyer on Mangrove Bend assigns her sales contract to her cousin, who then fails to close. Who is liable?
options: Only the cousin, since the rights were assigned
The buyer, because an assignor remains liable
No one, because the assignment discharged the contract
Only the seller, for allowing the assignment
question.why: With an assignment, the assignor stays liable if the assignee doesn't perform. Only a novation releases the original party.

cards.idea: Breach is failing to perform without legal excuse. Remedies are specific performance, compensatory damages, liquidated damages, or rescission. Specific performance exists because every parcel is unique, so money may not be enough; buyers usually seek it.
cards.scene: The buyer on Hibiscus Avenue walks away. The contract makes the $20,000 deposit liquidated damages. The seller keeps it and also wants to sue for the full loss. Having elected the deposit, that's the seller's whole remedy.
cards.trap: The exam offers keeping the deposit plus suing for more. If the contract makes the deposit liquidated damages and the seller elects to keep it, that's the entire remedy. No second bite.
cards.remember: A seller who keeps the deposit as liquidated damages gets nothing more.

question.q: A buyer on Hibiscus Avenue defaults. The contract makes the $20,000 deposit liquidated damages, and the seller elects to keep it. What else may the seller recover?
options: Nothing more, because the deposit is the whole remedy
Actual damages above the deposit
Specific performance in addition to the deposit
The deposit plus the full loss on resale
question.why: When the contract makes the deposit liquidated damages and the seller elects to keep it, that is the entire remedy. The seller can't also sue for the full loss.

cards.idea: Florida is a lien-theory state. The borrower keeps legal title, and the lender holds only a lien it enforces through court. The right to foreclose protects the lender, so it needs no title.
cards.scene: A buyer on Banyan Street finances 90 percent of the price. On closing day, he owns the house. The bank holds a recorded lien, not the deed.
cards.trap: The exam says the lender owns the property until the loan is paid off. That's title theory, not Florida. Here the borrower owns it from closing, and the lender has a lien.
cards.remember: Florida is lien theory: borrower holds title, lender holds a lien.

question.q: A buyer on Banyan Street finances most of the price with a bank loan. Under Florida law, who holds legal title after closing?
options: The bank, until the loan is paid off
A trustee, on behalf of the bank
The buyer, with the bank holding a lien
The buyer, until a default shifts title to the bank
question.why: Florida is a lien-theory state, so the borrower keeps legal title and the lender holds a lien. Lender title until payoff is title theory; title shifting on default is intermediate theory.

cards.idea: The note is the borrower's personal promise to repay: amount, rate, schedule, late terms. It's the evidence of the debt. It's negotiable, so the lender can sell it. In Florida, documentary stamp tax attaches to the note.
cards.scene: A borrower signs a note to a relative and pledges nothing. That's an unsecured debt: she's the maker, the relative is the payee. Only a second document, a mortgage pledging the house, makes it a mortgage loan.
cards.trap: The exam asks which document creates the personal obligation to repay and offers the mortgage. The answer is the note. The mortgage only pledges the house as security for the note's promise.
cards.remember: The note is the promise to pay. The mortgage is the pledge.

question.q: Which document creates the borrower's personal obligation to repay a home loan?
options: The mortgage
The promissory note
The deed
The satisfaction of mortgage
question.why: The promissory note is the borrower's promise to repay and the evidence of the debt. The mortgage pledges the property as security for that promise.

cards.idea: The mortgage pledges the property as security for the note and gives the lender the right to foreclose. In Florida it must be written, signed by the mortgagor, and recorded in the county where the property sits.
cards.scene: Daniela owns a house on Ridgewood Avenue in her own name, bought before marrying Tomas. They live there. She applies for a home equity loan alone. The title company insists Tomas sign the mortgage, because it's their homestead.
cards.trap: Two reversals. The exam says the mortgagee borrows; the borrower is the mortgagor, who gives the mortgage. And homestead doesn't protect the home from foreclosure on a mortgage the owners voluntarily signed.
cards.remember: Mortgagor borrows and gives. Mortgagee lends and receives. Homestead won't stop that foreclosure.

question.q: Daniela and Tomas live in her house on Ridgewood Avenue, their homestead. Both signed a mortgage on it, and they stop paying. Can the lender foreclose?
options: No, because homestead protects the home from forced sale
Yes, because homestead doesn't protect against a mortgage the owners signed
No, unless Tomas separately consents to the foreclosure
Yes, but only after the homestead status is removed
question.why: Homestead protects a Florida home from most creditors, but not from a mortgage the owners voluntarily signed. That lender can foreclose.

cards.idea: The exam tests mortgage clauses by name. Acceleration makes the whole balance due on default. Alienation, or due-on-sale, lets the lender call the loan on transfer. Defeasance releases the lien at payoff. Subordination puts the lien below a later one.
cards.scene: A developer borrows against twelve lots on Mangrove Circle under one blanket mortgage. Each time a lot sells, the partial release clause lets him pay down a set amount and deliver that lot free of the lien.
cards.trap: Acceleration and alienation both call the whole loan due, and the exam swaps them. Acceleration is triggered by default. Alienation is triggered by transfer, so a borrower current on every payment can still have the loan called.
cards.remember: Acceleration follows default. Alienation follows transfer.

question.q: A borrower who is current on every payment sells her house, and the lender demands the full loan balance. Which clause allows that?
options: Acceleration clause
Defeasance clause
Escalation clause
Alienation clause
question.why: The alienation, or due-on-sale, clause is triggered by a transfer of the property, even with no missed payments. Acceleration is triggered by default.

items.title: Buying a property that already has a mortgage

cards.idea: A buyer can pay off the seller's loan, take subject to it, or assume it. Subject to: no personal liability for the buyer. Assume: the buyer is personally liable. Either way the seller stays liable unless released, as by novation.
cards.scene: The Okafors sell on Seagrape Drive to a buyer who assumes their loan. Two years later he defaults, and the foreclosure sale falls short of the balance. The lender sues the Okafors for the shortfall, since it never released them.
cards.trap: The exam expects you to think assumption frees the seller. It doesn't; the seller stays secondarily liable. Only a novation releases the seller. And subject to means the buyer risks the house, not personal liability.
cards.remember: Subject to: buyer not personally liable. Assume: buyer liable. Only novation frees the seller.

question.q: The Okafors sell their house on Seagrape Drive to a buyer who assumes their loan, and the lender never releases them. The buyer defaults and the foreclosure sale falls short. Whom can the lender pursue?
options: Only the buyer, because he assumed the loan
Only the Okafors, as the original borrowers
No one, because the foreclosure sale settles the debt
The buyer, and then the Okafors
question.why: An assuming buyer is personally liable, and the seller stays secondarily liable unless the lender releases them. A novation would have freed the Okafors.

cards.idea: A lender can sell a loan by assigning the note and mortgage, recorded to show the new holder. The borrower's obligation doesn't change. At payoff, the lender must deliver a satisfaction, which the borrower records to clear the lien.
cards.scene: A homeowner pays off her loan, but the satisfaction of mortgage never gets recorded. Years later she sells. The title search for that sale flags the old lien as still open.
cards.trap: The exam treats payoff as the end of it. Payment ends the debt, but the lien stays on the public record until the satisfaction is recorded. An unrecorded satisfaction leaves a cloud on title.
cards.remember: Payment ends the debt. Recording the satisfaction clears the title.

question.q: A homeowner paid off her mortgage, but the satisfaction was never recorded. What will the title search for her next sale show?
options: An open lien still on record
No lien, because the debt was paid
A lien assigned to a new holder
A lis pendens against the property
question.why: Payment ends the debt, but the lien stays on the public record until the satisfaction is recorded. The title search will catch it as an open lien.

cards.idea: Florida is a judicial foreclosure state. Every residential foreclosure goes through circuit court: complaint and lis pendens, final judgment, then a public sale by the clerk. Court supervision is slower for lenders but gives borrowers time and a forum.
cards.scene: A homeowner on Cypress Bend falls behind in the spring. By the time the lis pendens is recorded, she has a buyer. She can still sell, pay the lender in full, and end the case, because the foreclosure sale hasn't happened.
cards.trap: The exam offers a trustee's sale with no court involvement. That's nonjudicial foreclosure, used in deed-of-trust states, not Florida. Also, Florida gives no statutory right to buy the house back after the sale.
cards.remember: Florida forecloses through court. Redemption runs until the clerk files the certificate of sale.

question.q: A lender wants to foreclose on a house on Cypress Bend. Which describes the Florida process?
options: A trustee sells the property under a power of sale, without court
The lender sues, and the clerk holds a public sale after final judgment
The lender takes title automatically once the borrower defaults
The lender sells, then the borrower has a statutory right to buy it back
question.why: Florida is a judicial foreclosure state: every residential foreclosure runs through circuit court and ends in the clerk's public sale. A trustee's sale without court is the nonjudicial method used in deed-of-trust states.

items.title: Deficiency judgments, deed in lieu, short sale

cards.idea: If the foreclosure sale brings less than the debt, Florida lets the lender seek a deficiency judgment against the borrower personally. A deed in lieu or a short sale avoids full foreclosure, but neither automatically ends that personal liability.
cards.scene: A seller on Tamarind Road owes $310,000, and the best offer is $285,000. The lender approves the short sale. Unless the approval letter waives the $25,000 shortfall, the lender can still pursue it.
cards.trap: The exam assumes a short sale or deed in lieu wipes out personal liability. It does only if the lender agrees in writing. Also, a deed in lieu leaves the lender subject to junior liens foreclosure would erase.
cards.remember: Short sale or deed in lieu: deficiency survives unless waived in writing.

question.q: A seller on Tamarind Road owes $310,000. The lender approves a $285,000 short sale, but the approval letter says nothing about the shortfall. What is true?
options: The short sale automatically cancels the $25,000 shortfall
The shortfall passes to the buyer at closing
The lender can still pursue the $25,000 shortfall
The lender must foreclose before it can recover anything
question.why: A short sale ends personal liability for the shortfall only if the lender agrees in writing to waive it. Without that, the lender can still pursue it.

cards.idea: The exam names the schemes: straw buyer, illegal flipping on a falsified appraisal, equity skimming, falsified income, and predatory loans built to profit from the borrower's failure. A licensee who knowingly joins faces federal criminal charges and license discipline.
cards.scene: Before closing, the seller plans to hand the buyer money on the side, calls it a gift, and wants it kept off the closing statement. The licensee who spots this has to refuse to take part.
cards.trap: The exam dresses hidden money up as a gift. Any money that changes hands in the deal and is hidden from the lender is mortgage fraud, whatever it's called.
cards.remember: Money hidden from the lender is mortgage fraud, whatever it's called.

question.q: A seller wants to give the buyer money toward the purchase, call it a gift, and keep it off the closing statement. What is this?
options: A permitted gift, since none of it goes to the licensee
Equity skimming, because the seller gives up equity
Mortgage fraud, because the money is hidden from the lender
A private matter between buyer and seller
question.why: Any money that changes hands in the deal and is hidden from the lender is mortgage fraud, whatever it is called. The licensee must refuse to take part.

cards.idea: RESPA bans kickbacks and referral fees. TILA requires APR disclosure and polices credit ads. TRID's Loan Estimate goes out within three business days of application. ECOA bars lending discrimination. In Florida, the Office of Financial Regulation licenses mortgage professionals.
cards.scene: A sales associate selling a condo on Banyan Street posts an ad: Only $9,000 down, 30-year financing. Both are specific credit terms. Now the ad must carry the APR and other required disclosures, or it violates Regulation Z.
cards.trap: The exam offers TILA's three-business-day right of rescission on a purchase loan. It never applies there. It covers certain refinances and home equity loans on a primary residence the borrower already owns.
cards.remember: No rescission right on the loan used to buy the home.

question.q: A buyer closes on a loan to purchase her home on Banyan Street. The next day she wants out of the loan. What does TILA give her?
options: A three-business-day right of rescission
A three-business-day right, if she hasn't moved in yet
Rescission until the Closing Disclosure is recorded
No right of rescission on a purchase loan
question.why: TILA's three-business-day rescission right covers certain refinances and home equity loans on a primary residence already owned. It never applies to the loan used to buy the home.

13.name: Types of Mortgages and Sources of Financing

cards.idea: How principal comes back defines the loan. Fully amortized reaches zero on the last payment. A term loan pays interest only, principal due at the end. A balloon leaves a lump sum at maturity. Graduated payments can cause negative amortization.
cards.scene: A seller on Jacaranda Way carries a $90,000 note, payments figured as if over 30 years, with the whole remaining balance due in year five. That's a balloon, so the buyer must plan to refinance before the balloon date.
cards.trap: The exam describes negative amortization without naming it: a payment that doesn't cover the interest. The wrong answer says the balance still drops slowly. It doesn't; unpaid interest is added, so the balance grows.
cards.remember: Payment below the interest means the balance grows: negative amortization.

question.q: In the early years of a graduated payment mortgage, the monthly payment doesn't cover the interest due. What happens to the loan balance?
options: It decreases slowly
It stays the same
It increases
It resets to the original amount
question.why: The unpaid interest is added to the balance, which is negative amortization. The borrower ends up owing more than they borrowed.

cards.idea: A fixed-rate loan keeps one rate for life. An ARM's rate follows an outside index plus the lender's fixed margin, resetting each adjustment period. Caps limit each move and the lifetime total.
cards.scene: A buyer on Pelican Point Road takes an ARM: index at 4.25 percent, margin 2.5 percent, so the fully indexed rate is 6.75 percent. If the index rises to 5 percent at adjustment, the rate becomes 7.5 percent, subject to caps.
cards.trap: The exam asks which part changes and offers the lender raising the margin. Wrong. The index moves. The margin, the lender's markup, stays fixed for the life of the loan.
cards.remember: Index moves, margin stays. Index plus margin is the rate.

question.q: A buyer on Pelican Point Road has an ARM with a 2.5 percent margin. At adjustment the index rises from 4.25 to 5 percent. What is the new rate, before caps?
options: 6.75 percent
7.5 percent
5 percent
4.25 percent
question.why: The rate is index plus margin, so 5 plus 2.5 is 7.5 percent. The margin stays fixed; only the index moved.

items.title: Conventional loans and private mortgage insurance

cards.idea: A conventional loan isn't insured or guaranteed by government, so the lender carries the risk. With a small down payment, customarily a loan above 80 percent of value, the lender usually requires PMI, which protects the lender against default.
cards.scene: A buyer on Royal Poinciana Drive puts 10 percent down on a conventional loan and pays PMI from day one. With good payment history she can ask to cancel at 80 percent of original value. At 78 percent, it drops off automatically.
cards.trap: The exam offers PMI as protection for a borrower who loses a job, or as payoff if the borrower dies. That's credit life or mortgage life insurance. PMI protects only the lender.
cards.remember: PMI protects the lender. It ends automatically at 78 percent.

question.q: A buyer on Royal Poinciana Drive puts 10 percent down on a conventional loan and pays PMI. Whom does the PMI protect?
options: The buyer, if she loses her job
The buyer's heirs, by paying off the loan at her death
The lender, against loss on default
The seller, until the sale closes
question.why: PMI protects the lender against loss if the borrower defaults. Coverage for job loss or death describes credit life or mortgage life insurance.

cards.idea: FHA, part of HUD, doesn't lend. It insures loans made by approved lenders. Hallmarks: low down payment, an up-front and annual mortgage insurance premium, owner occupancy, no prepayment penalty, assumable by a qualified buyer, county loan limits.
cards.scene: A first-time buyer on Osprey Lane with modest savings and solid income qualifies for an FHA loan on a $250,000 townhouse. At 3.5 percent, the down payment is $8,750. The up-front premium is added to the loan.
cards.trap: The exam says FHA loans the money. It doesn't; a bank or mortgage company lends, and FHA insures. And FHA's premium is MIP, while the conventional version is PMI.
cards.remember: FHA insures, never lends. FHA charges MIP; conventional loans use PMI.

question.q: A buyer on Osprey Lane gets an FHA loan for a townhouse. What is FHA's role in the loan?
options: It insures the loan made by an approved lender
It lends the money directly to the buyer
It guarantees a portion of the loan
It buys the loan on the secondary market
question.why: FHA doesn't lend; it insures loans made by approved lenders, so the lender is repaid on default. Guaranteeing a portion of the loan is what VA does.

cards.idea: The VA guarantees part of a loan made by an approved lender to an eligible veteran, servicemember, or certain surviving spouses. No down payment needed if the price stays within the VA appraisal and entitlement is full. No PMI. Assumable.
cards.scene: A Navy veteran stationed in Jacksonville buys on Lantana Avenue with no money down. Later he sells to a civilian who assumes the VA loan. Unless the VA releases him, he's still liable, and his entitlement stays tied up.
cards.trap: The exam swaps insured and guaranteed. FHA insures; VA guarantees. And the VA guaranty protects the lender, not the veteran, who stays liable after an assumption unless released.
cards.remember: VA guarantees, FHA insures. Both protect the lender.

question.q: A veteran on Lantana Avenue sells to a civilian who assumes his VA loan. The VA does not release him. What is his position?
options: He's free of the loan, because the guaranty protects him
He's liable only for the funding fee
His entitlement is restored once the buyer assumes
He's still liable, and his entitlement stays tied up
question.why: The VA guaranty protects the lender, not the veteran. Without a release of liability he stays liable, and his entitlement stays committed unless a qualified veteran buyer substitutes theirs.

cards.idea: A purchase-money mortgage is any mortgage that finances buying the property itself. On the exam it usually means the seller financing part of the price. In Florida, seller-held loans owe the same documentary stamp and intangible taxes as bank loans.
cards.scene: An owner sells a duplex on Hibiscus Court for $400,000, takes $80,000 down, and holds a $320,000 purchase-money mortgage. The note and mortgage are stamped and taxed at recording exactly as a bank's would be.
cards.trap: The exam suggests purchase-money means only a seller loan. A bank loan used to buy the house is purchase-money too. The phrase describes what the money buys, not who lends it.
cards.remember: Purchase-money describes what the loan buys, not who lends it.

question.q: A buyer finances her home purchase with a loan from a commercial bank. Is that a purchase-money mortgage?
options: Yes, because it finances the purchase itself
No, because only seller financing is purchase-money
No, because a bank loan is a conventional mortgage instead
Yes, but only if the seller also carries a note
question.why: A purchase-money mortgage is any mortgage given to finance buying the property. The phrase describes what the money buys, not who lends it.

cards.idea: Each specialty mortgage solves one problem. Blanket covers several parcels. Package covers real and personal property together. Wraparound keeps the seller's loan in place inside a bigger one. Reverse pays owners 62 or older against their equity.
cards.scene: A retired couple on Magnolia Bluff own their house outright and need income. A reverse mortgage pays them monthly. They make no payments; the balance is repaid from the sale after they leave the home.
cards.trap: The exam swaps blanket and package. Blanket covers more than one property, like a developer's lots. Package covers more than one kind of property, real plus personal, such as a furnished condo.
cards.remember: Blanket: many parcels. Package: real and personal property together.
